The procedure: sulcular incisions and a full-thickness flap; clean the exposed root (by hand instruments, ultrasonics or rotary instruments; without this nothing regenerates); remove enamel projections or pearls; fill the furcation with bone graft and/or cover it with a GTR membrane secured by a resorbable sling suture; secure the flap coronally; then no mechanical plaque removal at the site for up to 4 weeks, using chlorhexidine instead. Success is judged on a radiograph about a year later, as bone fill.

Tunneling deliberately removes bone from the furcation to make a tunnel through it, surgically creating a Glickman Grade IV, so the patient can pass an interproximal brush through. It's for deep Class II and Class III defects and is limited to mandibular molars with sufficiently long, divergent roots. Its problem: caries in tunneled molars is common, since root surfaces decay quickly. It's rarely done now that implants exist.

Root resection (root amputation) removes one or more roots at the level of the furcation while the crown and remaining roots stay in function. The most common root removed is the distobuccal root of the maxillary first molar. It's limited to deep Class II and Class III defects, aims to eliminate the furcation as a maintenance problem, and commits the patient to endodontic and restorative treatment. It's still used, for example when the bridge abutment #31, already root-canal treated, fractures its mesial root while the distal root is sound: the fractured root is removed and the bridge is kept. Hemisection removes a root and the associated part of the crown, usually on mandibular molars, turning a multi-rooted tooth into a single-rooted one. Implants have made it much less common: it means an endodontist, then the periodontist, then the restorative dentist, over many expensive visits.

The sequence for root separation or resection: endodontic treatment first, with the access filled directly with amalgam or composite; a provisional restoration; then root separation and resection, avoiding exposing the interradicular bone, leaving parts of the furcation fornix behind, perforating the canals, or leaving sharp angles on the remaining roots; periodontal surgery to remove bone defects around the remaining roots, with provisional margins ending at least 3 mm coronal to the bone crest; and the final restoration, with a rigid framework for the weakened abutments and an occlusion that minimizes lateral forces.

In class: the furcation points he repeated

Before the new material, Dr. Litz went back over the recorded lecture. A furcation is normal anatomy; the problem is a furcation defect, and once a furcation is involved the prognosis of the tooth dramatically falls, because we can barely clean it and the patient almost never can. He asked again for the entrance numbers ("I want you to know these numbers"): maxillary first molar mesiopalatal 3.6, buccal 4.2, distopalatal 4.8 mm; mandibular buccal 2.4 and lingual 2.5 mm. So when a molar probes 4, 5 or 6 mm, assume one or more furcations are already exposed. Most entrances are narrower than a curette blade, and every root surface facing into the furcation is concave, which hides calculus where a convex root hands it to you. Asked why maxillary molars break down, he pointed to their less dense bone and their thin facial bone, since these molars tend to sit pushed toward the facial. A thin cervical enamel projection usually comes off with a finishing bur, such as a 7404, in light feather strokes; warn the patient about thermal sensitivity if it's thick. One isolated deep site in an otherwise healthy mouth means something is going on with that one tooth: a CEP, an overhang, residual cement, or a vertically fractured root on a root-canal-treated molar, which means the tooth comes out. He finds furcations with a Nabers probe on every multi-rooted tooth and prefers the Glickman classes, which the school uses too.

Phase I, re-evaluation and when surgery comes in

In general dentistry, Phase I removes active disease (extract hopeless teeth, endodontics, periodontal therapy) and Phase II is restorative. In periodontics, Phase I is oral hygiene instruction (always first), scaling and root planing, control of plaque-retentive features (overhanging margins, open contacts, odontoplasty for things like CEPs, often only reachable once a flap is raised) and the Phase I re-evaluation. Phase II is surgery, followed by periodontal maintenance (supportive periodontal therapy, recall). Phase I aims to reduce or eliminate gingival inflammation, eliminate pockets produced by edematous enlargement of inflamed gingiva, create an environment that the patient can keep clean, which he called the therapeutic goal for almost every patient (we clean their teeth two to four times a year; they clean them 700 to 800), and improve the surgical manageability of the tissue: firm, with minimal bleeding. That is why a patient can't skip Phase I and go straight to surgery, even one you know will need it: a surgeon clears an infected laceration before setting the fracture under it, and inflamed gingiva bleeds heavily and shreds when a flap is raised.

The re-evaluation comes about 4 to 6 weeks after Phase I, when root planing has had its maximum effect, the flora is most favorable and hygiene is at its best. It asks: Is initial therapy complete (etiologic factors controlled, adequate hygiene, no plaque or calculus, inflammation controlled, reduced probing depths)? Is the periodontal status maintainable (shallow or deep pockets, remaining attachment, esthetics, challenges during maintenance)? Can the patient benefit from Phase II surgery: resective surgery, regeneration, open flap debridement or soft-tissue grafting? Three paths follow. Shallow pockets and good hygiene: periodontal maintenance every 3 to 4 months. Plaque everywhere, bleeding and pockets: back through Phase I, reviewing hygiene and debriding again. Good hygiene but deep pockets that a brush and floss can't reach: a surgical candidate.

The treatment goals: control plaque to a level compatible with health, eliminate contributing risk factors (furcations, CEPs, overhangs), arrest the disease and prevent recurrence. His slides list 11 indications for periodontal surgery, led by access for root debridement and pocket elimination by removing soft or hard tissue; the others are removing diseased tissue to favor new attachment, correcting mucogingival defects, contours that make hygiene easier, esthetics, a favorable restorative environment, drainage of acute problems, exploratory procedures to determine the prognosis, biopsy, and regeneration. Access matters because root planing has limits. A 1981 study he still cites found a high correlation between residual calculus and pocket depth: in 3 to 5 mm pockets the chance of failure becomes greater, and over 5 mm failure dominates, for three reasons: more surface area to clean, more irregularities as the pocket deepens (furcations at 3.6, 4.2 and 4.8 mm), and an apical part that narrows until the bottom can't be reached. A flap lets you see the root, like doing a filling with your eyes open.

Osseous surgery: why remove bone

The primary objective of osseous surgery is to eliminate periodontal pockets and create a shallow gingival sulcus the patient can keep clean, with a bony architecture that matches a physiologic gingival architecture. Gingiva is scalloped, like a child's drawing of ocean waves, higher interproximally and lower on the midfacial, and it returns to that shape after surgery even if the bone underneath does not. His most important slide: if the bone does not follow the overlying gingival architecture, the pockets will recur. Ochsenbein defined resective surgery as a procedure to eliminate bony deformities so that bone and gingiva are consistent with each other and the pocket is reduced or eliminated. Treating bone loss by removing bone sounds backwards, he said, but sometimes you fight fire with fire.

Periodontitis leaves an uneven bone crest and deep pockets, especially where bone is lost vertically between teeth. In health, the interproximal crest sits about 1 to 2 mm from the adjacent CEJs on a radiograph. Normal alveolar bone has three features: the interproximal bone is more coronal than the labial or lingual bone and pyramidal; the shape of the interdental bone follows the tooth form and embrasure width; and the bony margin mimics the contour of the CEJ. In positive architecture the interproximal crest is coronal to its midfacial and midlingual height, the healthy pattern and the goal. In negative (reverse) architecture it is apical, a crater with deep pockets between the teeth. Flat architecture lies between. When reaching positive architecture would mean removing too much facial and lingual bone, as around a deep interproximal defect between #28 and #29, he settles for flat rather than weaken the tooth.

The cost is small. Properly performed osseous surgery removes on average about 0.6 mm of supporting bone height around the tooth. Bone is taken from the facial and lingual or palatal, and interproximal bone is preserved, because the facial and lingual surfaces are smaller, so removing bone there costs less support. Teeth are more mobile after osseous resection, but mobility returns to pre-operative levels after about a year (Selipsky, 1976); warn the patient beforehand.

Indications and contraindications

Resective surgery is indicated to gain access to an underlying structure (a CEP, a furcation), to remove subgingival bacteria and calculus more effectively, and to reduce or eliminate persistent diseased sites, including bony defects that don't follow the gingival architecture. In practice: active periodontitis that Phase I failed to eradicate; moderate to severe pockets with limited improvement after root planing (the slides say over 4 mm and in furcations; in class he put the line at about 5 mm); mild to moderate horizontal bone loss; 2-wall crater defects and shallow 1-, 2- and 3-wall defects; better access to shallow furcation defects; removing ledges and exostoses such as buccal exostoses and lingual tori, where the gingiva meets the tooth at almost a right angle and can't be cleaned; and creating positive architecture. The goal at the root is a knife-edge approximation of bone to tooth and convex rather than concave contours.

The contraindications: ineffective plaque control, the big one ("there's not a periodontist on this earth that doesn't know this"), which the re-evaluation is there to catch, since surgery cures nothing and only creates an environment the patient can keep clean; noncompliance with the treatment plan, such as wanting to skip Phase I; shallow pockets, where surgery or root planing causes attachment loss; a hard-tissue defect amenable to regeneration, which should be regenerated instead (Session 6); an anticipated unacceptable cosmetic result, such as long maxillary anterior teeth in a patient with a high smile line; and uncontrolled systemic disease.

Ostectomy, osteoplasty and the steps

Ostectomy removes tooth-supporting bone, the alveolar bone proper that is part of the attachment apparatus, to reach a more physiologic form. Osteoplasty reshapes the alveolar process without removing supporting bone: bone with no attachment to the tooth, so it can be thinned more aggressively, even on the facial, as long as it doesn't touch the root (Friedman, 1955). The steps: 1. vertical grooving interproximally (osteoplasty, with large round burs such as a #6 or #8), 2. radicular blending, 3. flattening the interproximal bone, and 4. gradualizing the marginal bone, the conservative ostectomy on the facial and lingual that brings back positive architecture. The most important step of all is thorough debridement of the root surfaces: "if these are not clean root surfaces, nothing is going to work," whether you reshape bone or graft it.

Around maxillary molars, treat the mesiobuccal and distobuccal roots as if they were separate teeth: remove bone on the facial of each root, but never take down the bone in the furcation. Exposing it lowers the prognosis, and that bone is hard to get back. Flaps are closed with silk sutures, removed after a week. Patients should know what to expect: longer teeth, exposed roots with possible thermal sensitivity (topical agents help), and open embrasures that trap some food but can now be cleaned with interproximal brushes. His resident case was a three-unit bridge from #3 to #5 that the patient couldn't clean under; bridges are among the most breakdown-prone areas in any mouth. After Phase I, surgery corrected the flat and negative architecture while preserving the furcation bone, and six months later the gingiva was healthy and an interproximal brush fit under the pontic: the whole point of the procedure. And if the patient doesn't clean, none of it works.
full.periodontal-regeneration:
These notes come from Dr. Geurs' slide deck, posted ahead of the lecture, plus the class exam-review guide. His two learning objectives: case selection for regeneration, and what you can achieve with regenerative techniques.

What regeneration means

The definition on the slides comes from the 1996 World Workshop in Clinical Periodontics: periodontal regeneration is the formation of new bone, new cementum and new periodontal ligament, together forming a new functional attachment apparatus, over a pathologically exposed root surface. All three tissues are required; bone fill alone is not regeneration. The slide sets regeneration against repair, healing that does not restore the original architecture and function. After a flap or root planing, a root usually heals by repair: a long junctional epithelium lies against the root instead of new cementum with inserting ligament fibers.

What it takes

The deck lists four factors in periodontal tissue repair and regeneration: cells, scaffolds, growth factors and blood supply. The cells have to come from the PDL and bone next to the defect, a scaffold gives them something to grow into and holds the space, growth factors recruit them and make them multiply, and a blood supply keeps the clot and the new tissue alive. The deck's map of strategies (Wang, 2022, on cell and cell-free therapies) splits the field in two. Tissue engineering brings cells in: cell suspensions or aggregates, cells expanded outside the body, and cells seeded onto materials or scaffolds, which can be electrospun or 3D printed. Endogenous regeneration is cell-free: it mobilizes the patient's own cells and draws them to the site (cell homing) with biological factors, extracellular matrix, exosomes and microvesicles, or drugs. Everything in the deck's cases is the second kind: grafts, membranes and biologics that work with the patient's own cells.

Case selection: defect morphology

Infrabony defects are classified by the number of bony walls, their width and their depth (Reynolds, AAP Regeneration Workshop, 2015). The classification drawing numbers the walls in each zone: one defect often combines them, with three walls deep in the defect and fewer toward the crest, and a 1-wall defect between two teeth is a hemiseptum. Defects with a depth greater than 3 mm and a radiographic defect angle of 25 degrees or less were reported to be most amenable to conventional GTR-based regeneration. A 2021 systematic review (Nibali) agrees: deeper defects with narrower angles and more walls showed more CAL gain and radiographic bone gain 12 months after regenerative surgery. In its pooled numbers, defects shallower than 4 mm gained about 0.75 mm less bone, defects with an angle under 37 degrees about 0.94 mm more, and a 1-wall defect about 1.2 mm less bone than a 3-wall one (about 0.6 mm less than a 2-wall). Depth had the strongest evidence. The walls and a narrow angle contain the defect: they hold the clot and graft in place, bring cells and blood vessels in from more surfaces, and hold up the flap. The exam-review guide puts it simply: 3-wall defects are the best candidates.

Non-supportive anatomy, defined as a predominantly 1-wall defect, is a risk factor for failure, with an odds ratio of 10.4 or more. In a 2012 study of minimally invasive surgery with a collagen-enriched bovine xenograft (Cosyn), a 1-wall rather than 2-wall defect and a thin, scalloped gingival biotype were the risk factors for more recession at the midfacial after surgery. A radiograph is a flat picture of a three-dimensional defect: the deck's dry-skull films of 3-, 2- and 1-wall defects on the same molar (Zengin, 2015) show how hard the walls are to tell apart on a film. So the walls are confirmed at surgery, once the flap is raised and the defect is debrided, as in the deck's opening case, shown from the buccal, from the lingual and after debridement.

Risk assessment and the decision tree

The periodontal regeneration risk assessment for intrabony defects (Levine, 2023) rates four groups of factors as low, medium or high risk. Patient factors: medical status (healthy, uneventful healing is low; compromised healing is high); smoking (a nonsmoker is low, a light smoker of 10 cigarettes a day or fewer is medium, more than 10 a day is high); plaque control by full-mouth plaque score (15% or less is low, 16 to 24% medium, 25% or more high); compliance with supportive periodontal care (compliant, erratic or poor); and realistic or unrealistic expectations. Tooth factors: the site's periodontal risk score; whether occlusal trauma and mobility are controllable; the endodontic condition (a vital tooth whose defect doesn't reach the apex, or adequate root canal treatment, is low; existing root canal therapy needs careful evaluation and is medium; a defect reaching the apex of a vital tooth, inadequate root canal treatment or a nonvital tooth is high); the root surface (flat is low, concave medium, two fused roots high); intact soft tissue or soft-tissue defects; and the gingival phenotype (thick is low; thin with a band of keratinized tissue 2 mm or wider is medium; thin with a narrow band or none is high). Defect factors: a 3-wall, narrow, deep defect is low, a 2-wall defect medium, and a 1-wall, wide, shallow defect high; no furcation involvement is low, Class I or II medium, Class III high; the defect must be cleansable through surgical access (anterior is low, posterior medium); and a contained defect, with 1 or 2 sides of the root involved, is low, while a non-contained defect, with 3 or more sides involved, is high. Operator factors: experience, environmental stress, and whether a checklist is used.

The decision tree from the AAP Regeneration Workshop (Reynolds, 2015) starts with the patient: address first uncontrolled systemic conditions, tobacco use and other behavioral issues, and inadequate oral hygiene. These are the same factors that ruled furcation regeneration out in Session 5. After initial therapy and any occlusal trauma or mobility management, assess the site: probing depth and CAL, bleeding on probing, mobility and fremitus, the osseous architecture clinically and on radiographs, and any restorative, endodontic or orthodontic work. An intrabony defect under 3 mm isn't a regeneration case: with probing depths of 5 mm or less and no bleeding, consider non-surgical management; with probing depths over 5 mm, consider osseous surgery. For a defect of 3 mm or more, predictability runs 3-wall, then circumferential or 2-wall, then 1-wall, and narrow beats wide. If the prognosis with treatment is unfavorable, or poor to hopeless, the answer is extraction and tooth replacement. Otherwise regeneration follows the defect: a 3-wall or circumferential defect under 2 mm wide takes a bone graft, a GTR membrane or a biologic; one 3 mm or wider, or a 2-wall defect, takes a reinforced GTR membrane, a bone graft plus a GTR membrane, or a bone graft plus a biologic; a 1-wall defect takes combination therapy or a cellular bone allograft. Esthetic risk is weighed alongside. With low risk (a low smile line, a thick biotype, a full papilla, under 5 mm from the contact to the interproximal bone crest), proceed. With high risk (a high smile line, a thin biotype, papilla loss or more than 6 mm from the contact to the crest), proceed only if the patient accepts the esthetic risk, avoid a GTR membrane, and consider soft-tissue augmentation.

The toolbox

Regenerative procedures aim at new bone, cementum and PDL, and at attachment gain, in infrabony defects, 2- and 3-wall. The deck lists bone grafts, guided tissue regeneration (GTR), combination therapy, biomodification with enamel matrix proteins or PDGF, and MIST, the minimally invasive surgical technique, which works through a small flap that keeps the papilla. Regenerative therapy rebuilds the lost support; resective therapy, from Session 5, reshapes the bone to eliminate the pocket instead.

Bone grafts. The deck's graft case used DFDBA, demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft: bone from a human tissue-bank donor. The defect was filled, and after healing the site probed 3 mm. Grafts are named by where they come from: an autograft from the patient, an allograft from another human, a xenograft from another species, such as bovine bone, and an alloplast, a synthetic material such as beta-tricalcium phosphate.

Guided tissue regeneration. A barrier membrane goes over the defect, under the flap. It keeps the fast-growing gingival epithelium and connective tissue off the root, so cells from the PDL and bone can repopulate it. In combination therapy a bone graft goes under the membrane and holds the space, so the membrane can't collapse into the defect. The deck follows GTR and graft cases with radiographs at 1 year, 20 years and 25 years: the regenerated bone was still there decades later.

Biologics. Enamel matrix derivative (EMD) is an extract of enamel matrix proteins, mostly amelogenins, the proteins involved in enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during tooth development. Used alone or with a graft, it gives outcomes similar to GTR; the deck shows a case healing with EMD from 2022 to 2025. rhPDGF-BB, recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor BB, is chemotactic and mitogenic for bone and PDL cells and angiogenic, so it drives revascularization. A beta-TCP scaffold is an osteoconductive matrix that keeps soft tissue from collapsing into the defect and stabilizes the clot; the exam-review guide pairs it with rhPDGF-BB.

Non-contained defects. The deck gives a slide to treating non-contained infrabony defects (Journal of Periodontology, 2017). Its photos follow one case from the radiograph through the flap, debridement, the graft packed into the defect and the sutures to the follow-up radiograph. Without walls, nothing holds up the flap or the clot, so a biologic alone has no space to work in; these defects usually get a graft as well, to support the soft tissue, which is why the decision tree sends a 1-wall defect to combination therapy.

What can you achieve?

The baseline is open flap debridement alone. Across four studies on the slide (Froum 1981, Renvert 1985, Yukna 1985 and Laurell's 1998 meta-analysis), defects 3.4 to 4.3 mm deep started at probing depths of about 6.3 to 7.4 mm and ended at about 3.5 to 4.1 mm, with 1.3 to 1.5 mm of CAL gain and 0.7 to 1.2 mm of bone gain. Laurell's meta-analysis of 305 defects: probing depth 7.0 to 4.0 mm, CAL gain 1.5 mm, bone gain 1.1 mm. The probing depth fell 3 mm but the attachment level only 1.5 mm, because the rest of the pocket reduction is recession. Regenerative techniques are judged by how much they add to this baseline. The deck's results slide shows four combinations healing on radiographs between 3 and 16 months: Emdogain with DFDBA, GTR with autogenous bone, rhPDGF with DFDBA, and DFDBA alone.

Proving it worked

Regeneration is evaluated three ways: histology, clinical measurements and radiographs. Only histology, a section of the tooth with its surrounding tissue, can show new cementum with inserting PDL fibers and new bone, and so prove true regeneration; the deck shows histological evidence of regeneration in intrabony defects. A probe can't tell new attachment from a long junctional epithelium, and a radiograph shows bone fill, not attachment. Digital subtraction radiography lines up two standardized radiographs taken at different times and subtracts one from the other, so only what changed shows. Dr. Geurs and colleagues used it to evaluate a bioresorbable membrane in periodontal bone defects (Chaves, Geurs, Reddy and Jeffcoat, 1996): the subtraction image lights up the bone gained at the distal site between the presurgical film and the one at 6 months. In the same study, histology 6 months after the membrane showed new cementum, a periodontal ligament space and new bone formed into a reference notch cut in the root.
full.implants-perio:
Dr. Kaur taught this session in class on Oct 29 (the class capture) with her updated slide deck. Her question for the session: are dental implants contraindicated in periodontally compromised patients? Her answer at the end: no, not once the periodontitis is treated, arrested and the patient is compliant. On the way there she built the picture of peri-implant health and disease the same way you already picture periodontal health, gingivitis and periodontitis.

Success versus survival

"Be cautious of the terms used, success versus survival." A surviving implant is simply present in the mouth and restored, in other words loaded. A surviving implant can still have biologic complications (peri-implant mucositis, peri-implantitis, bone loss, inflammation) and prosthetic complications (a fractured abutment, a loose screw, a fractured crown, even a fractured implant), or simply pain or mucosal recession. A successful implant is restored and free of any complication, clinically and radiographically. When you read implant studies, check which one they measured.

The success criteria on the slide are Albrektsson's, from 1986: the implant is immobile; there is no peri-implant radiolucency; there is no pain, infection, paresthesia or neuropathy; and after 1 year in function, vertical bone loss is 1.5 mm or less. In class she added the rest of the criterion: after that first year, no more than 0.2 mm of vertical bone loss a year. A radiolucency at the apical third of an implant is called retrograde peri-implantitis.

The 2017 classification: peri-implant health and disease

From 1986 to 2017 there was no agreed classification of health and disease around implants. The 2017 World Workshop added one alongside the new periodontal classification: peri-implant health, peri-implant mucositis, peri-implantitis, and peri-implant soft and hard tissue deficiencies.

Peri-implant health. No clinical signs of inflammation (no change in color, no edema, no redness); no bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; no increase in probing depth compared with previous examinations; and no bone loss beyond the crestal bone level changes from initial remodeling. Notice there is no 3 mm cutoff. A healthy implant can probe deeper than 3 mm: the tissue height around it depends on how deep the implant was placed, the height of the abutment, and the tissue itself (a narrow implant in a wide ridge leaves extra tissue). Probing an implant is also hard to do accurately, even with a plastic probe. So every measurement is compared with that implant's own baseline: capture the clinical and radiographic baseline, or you will have nothing to compare to going forward.

Crestal remodeling. Once an implant is put in function, the crestal bone adapts to the new load. In class she put a number on it, which the slide doesn't: about 2 mm of remodeling, which plateaus within about the first year. That is physiologic. Any bone loss beyond it is pathologic.

Peri-implant mucositis, the implant's version of gingivitis. Signs of inflammation; profuse (line or drop) bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; an increase in probing depth compared with baseline; and no bone loss beyond initial remodeling. The deeper pocket comes from inflamed, swollen tissue, not from bone loss. Like gingivitis it is reversible, so take it seriously: don't just put it on watch. A probing depth can only grow for three reasons: an inaccurate measurement, inflammation adding volume to the tissue, or true bone loss.

Suppuration (pus) is a sign of active disease, around a tooth or an implant, and it always needs a response now, whatever the long-term plan: local debridement, and sometimes a local antibiotic at a deep site (Dr. Litz covers antibiotics in Session 8).

Peri-implantitis. Signs of inflammation; bleeding and/or suppuration on gentle probing; increased probing depth compared with previous exams; and bone loss beyond the crestal changes from initial remodeling. "When somebody talks about peri-implantitis, you should have a picture of true bone loss in your mind." The definition on the slide: a plaque-associated pathological condition in the tissues around implants, characterized by inflammation in the peri-implant mucosa and subsequent progressive loss of supporting bone. The definition itself says the disease runs from inflammation to bone loss, which is why it must be controlled at the mucositis stage.

Why is it so hard to treat? Rebuilding bone around an implant should be easier than true periodontal regeneration: there is no PDL or cementum to regrow, only bone fill, so only osteoblasts are needed. The problem is the surface. Implants are made rough (acid-etched, blasted), even nano-rough, because osteoblasts love it, and so does plaque. No product is better than another at decontaminating the implant surface: saline, chlorhexidine (Peridex), citric acid, EDTA and lasers give the same or similar results. Bone loss around implants also tends not to form the deep, narrow, vertical defects that regenerate best, and disease recurs often. Still, a case with a deep buccal pocket (8-9 mm), suppuration, bleeding and bone loss, but with the mesial and distal bone peaks and the lingual plate intact, is still worth treating: open it, clean it, place a biologic and/or bone graft, cover it with a barrier membrane and close.

Peri-implant soft and hard tissue deficiency is loss of the mucosa along with the bone under it. Often bone is lost while the mucosal margin stays put; with a long-standing disease or risk factors such as a thin phenotype, which recedes faster than a thick one, the tissue goes too.

Ailing, failing, failed (Meffert 1992)

This classification describes the implant's state and tells you what to do. An ailing implant has static radiographic bone loss with no inflammation and no mobility: the loss stopped, on its own or because someone intervened. Monitor it, and capture the clinical and radiographic data at each visit. A failing implant has progressive bone loss and signs of inflammation, but no mobility: it is still in function, and what you do varies case by case (for example, keep an 89-year-old's implants at #18 and #19 when taking them out would leave too little bone above the inferior alveolar nerve to rebuild). A failed implant has progressive bone loss, clinical mobility and loss of function. Unlike a tooth, a mobile implant has only one treatment: remove it. Mobility of the implant body means loss of osseointegration, which "nobody in this universe can reverse." First confirm the mobility is in the implant body, not the abutment or the crown.

Loss of osseointegration is usually not from peri-implantitis: implants rarely become mobile from peri-implantitis, even with only a third of the implant left in bone. An implant with bone loss that advanced is still judged failed, mobile or not, when it has no future.

Etiology, microbiology and risk factors

Peri-implant disease is multifactorial, but "if somebody has to ask you" how it starts, the answer is bacteria: plaque biofilm. Periodontitis and peri-implantitis share causative bacteria. The slide groups the risk factors as patient-related, surgical/implant-related, soft tissue and prosthetic.

Risk factors for peri-implant mucositis (slide): smoking (current or former), history of periodontitis, active periodontitis, thin soft tissue phenotype, and obesity and/or metabolic syndrome. Risk factors for peri-implantitis: smoking (current or former), history of periodontitis, active periodontitis, obesity and/or metabolic syndrome, implant malposition, uncontrolled diabetes, limited bone width, and depression or antidepressant medications. Poor plaque control carried an odds ratio of 14.3 (Ferreira et al. 2006). Other factors on the slide: systemic disease, lack of keratinized tissue and parafunctional habits.

Microbiology. The flora of the mouth before implantation determines the flora around the implant. The flora around stable implants resembles the subgingival flora of a healthy dentate patient. The etiology of peri-implantitis is probably multifactorial, and genetic factors play an important role. The pellicle starts forming on the implant as early as 30 minutes after it is exposed in the mouth. The early colonizers are mostly gram-positive cocci and rods, including Actinomyces, just as on teeth; as the biofilm matures, the periodontal pathogens (P. gingivalis, P. intermedia and others), gram-negative anaerobes, cause both peri-implantitis and periodontitis.

Why the patient lost their teeth matters

Yes, it matters. A patient who lost teeth to periodontitis is a susceptible host, and susceptibility to periodontal disease raises the risk of peri-implant disease, even in a fully edentulous mouth. Putative periodontal pathogens may persist even a year after periodontally involved teeth are extracted. Definitive treatment of periodontitis is critical to success, and untreated periodontitis is a contraindication to implant therapy. A patient whose periodontitis has been treated and is in maintenance can receive implants like anyone else, with a maintenance plan matched to their risk.

The order matters. For a patient with advanced bone loss and heavy calculus: scaling and root planing first; extract the hopeless teeth in the disease-control phase without immediate implants; let everything heal with good oral hygiene instructions; re-evaluate after Phase I; do any Phase II pocket elimination surgery; and only then plan implants, once pockets are reduced and the patient's hygiene has changed. Risk assessment happens again at placement, at the prosthetic phase and at every maintenance visit.

Two-stage and single-stage. In a two-stage implant, a cover screw closes the implant and the tissue is closed over it to heal. About 3-4 months later it is uncovered, a healing abutment (transmucosal: it comes through the mucosa) is attached, and after about 2-3 weeks the impression is made with a prosthetic abutment. In a single-stage implant the healing abutment goes on at placement, when bone and tissue are ideal, saving a second surgery.

The #31 case. A 41-year-old man with untreated periodontitis had implant #31 placed, with bone graft at the distal of #30, and then no follow-up or maintenance. The graft could not regenerate between avascular cementum and metal in a diseased mouth. Two years after placement he came back with food packing, his only complaint, and loss of hard and soft tissue around #31 (a peri-implant soft and hard tissue deficiency). The implant was removed with a reverse-torque tool. One option was a root canal and resection of #30's distal root, then grafting and a new #31 implant; the case was instead treated more aggressively: #30 was extracted with socket conversion, the ridge was rebuilt vertically, and implants were placed at #30 and #31. Extracting #30 gave the graft a high bone peak on the mesial to grow against.

The European Association for Osseointegration's 2006 Zurich consensus found significantly more peri-implantitis and marginal bone loss in people who lost teeth to periodontitis. In the study she showed (Roccuzzo 2010, 10 years) healthy, moderately and severely compromised patients were compared on survival alone, and the compromised groups lost more implants; complications would be higher still. Supportive peri-implant therapy (SPIT) follows the 2024 AO/AAP consensus.

Challenges of periodontally compromised patients

Periodontally compromised teeth have attachment loss, pockets, alveolar bone loss and tooth loss. For implants that means:

Soft tissue loss: papillary loss, black triangles and loss of keratinized tissue, more pronounced on the thin periodontium phenotype. Recession loses keratinized gingiva first, and the tissue's thickness changes too; both the amount of keratinized tissue and its thickness guide the implant's health. This matters most in the esthetic zone, where loss of hard and soft tissue can also come from trauma.

Reduced bone volume: biomechanical concerns, and implant fractures from an unfavorable crown-implant ratio. Bone width is far easier to grow than height. A sinus lift is relatively easy height, because the bone grows into the sinus, not into the mouth. In one case (missing #1-7, implants at #2, 3, 4 and 6) the vertical defect was too great: the anterior implants were lost and the patient, who wanted something fixed, ended up with a removable implant-supported prosthesis.

Bone grafting options (slide): socket conversion, ridge augmentation and sinus lifts; nerve repositioning or short implants; and distraction osteogenesis for vertical augmentation.

Risk assessment and risk factors

Risk assessment is done before implant placement, during the osseointegration period, during implant maintenance, and after the removal of an implant: at every stage, not once. Any risk factor that increases the risk of periodontitis also increases the risk of implant failure, and untreated or partially treated periodontal disease leads more often to implant failure.

Smoking works on three fronts. Microbiology: smokers harbor different, more virulent plaque bacteria, and A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis and B. forsythus are harder to eradicate in current smokers; smoking depletes oxygen, and the gram-negative anaerobes love that. Immunology: impaired neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis, fewer T helper cells and B lymphocytes, more IL-6 and TNF-alpha, and more collagenase activity. Physiology: nicotine impairs revascularization in soft and hard tissue, the first step of healing after surgery. The numbers: Bain and Moy 1993, 2,194 implants, failure rate 11.3% in smokers vs 4.76% in nonsmokers; Alsaadi 2007, a dose-response relationship, with worse rates in heavy smokers; Simonis 2010, peri-implantitis in 23.53% of smokers vs 16.51% of nonsmokers. Dose-response means the higher the dose, the worse the outcome: years of smoking and cigarettes a day both count, and risk starts below a pack (20) a day. Vaping: little long-term evidence; there is no combustion, so the vasoconstrictive effect on healing may be missing, but the immune response is still suppressed.

Diabetes. The duration of diabetes did not affect implant survival under optimal glycemic control. A periodontally healthy environment is essential along with good glycemic levels, and implant therapy is contraindicated with poorly controlled diabetes. The measure is glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c), the gold standard, because it reflects the last 3-4 months, the lifespan of red blood cells. Get the lab value for your records. (Not part of the lecture, she added: UAB's clinic uses an HbA1c of 8 or higher as a contraindication, and a patient's value can come down, so keep reassessing.)

From the class exam-review guide (not in this year's slides): IL-1 gene polymorphisms are linked to a hyper-responsive inflammatory reaction to bacteria, and a positive IL-1 genotype plus smoking has a synergistic effect, the highest peri-implantitis risk. In class she listed genetic traits and a family history of periodontitis among the risk factors to weigh.

Maintenance: probing, bleeding and radiographs

Implants are maintained with implant probes (plastic) and implant scalers, different from the SRP instruments; many healthy implants need little cleaning. The diagnostic criteria for peri-implant evaluation (Lang and Berglundh 2011): bleeding on probing (with a light force, about 0.25 N), soft tissue evaluation, suppuration, probing depth, pain or tenderness, mobility and radiographic bone loss.

Bleeding on probing depends on the tissue's condition and on the probing force. It can be caused by an inappropriate probing force or angulation, or by inflammation of the marginal tissue. Its absence is a good predictor of stable peri-implant conditions; its presence indicates inflammation but may not predict progression. Look at the type of bleeding: a little blood that appears slowly may not mean disease, but profuse bleeding that fills the sulcus as you probe does. Track it over visits. In the study on the slide, sites that bled at 4 of 4 visits had a 30% chance of attachment loss; 3 of 4, 14%; 2 of 4, 6%; 1 of 4, 3%; and sites with no bleeding at any of 4 visits, 1.5%. Bleeding on probing is a limited but useful prognostic indicator.

Radiographs are taken at: implant placement; before the Phase II uncovery surgery (or before the prosthetic phase if one-stage); the final impression; final abutment seating; the final cementation or restoration (the baseline radiograph); every 6 months for the first year; and annually after that. Extra radiographs are indicated at a maintenance visit when the clinical signs point to disease: increased probing depth, bleeding on probing, suppuration. "Radiographs are confirmatory rather than exploratory" (Lang and Hill 1977): read them together with the clinical findings.

Conclusions

Risk assessment and control of risk factors are an integral part of implant therapy. Discuss the increased risk of peri-implantitis with a patient who has a history of periodontal disease or other risk factors. Treat any periodontal infection before starting implant therapy. Compliance with plaque control and regular maintenance decides the result, and much of it is in the patient's hands: make them your co-therapist. A treated, arrested, compliant patient with a history of periodontitis is not a contraindication for implants.
full.antibiotics-host-mod:
Dr. Matthew Litz gave this session in two parts. He recorded the antibiotics half ("I give this lecture every year to the dental students"; the file posted is dated March 2024), then taught host modulation in class on Nov 5, after a short recap of the antibiotics. The antibiotics notes come from the recording, the slides and that recap; the host modulation section comes from the class. He boiled the lecture down to "the most basic information that I feel like you need when you start treating patients in the clinic."

Bacteria cause it, but antibiotics are only for select cases

Periodontal disease is initiated by a relatively specific group of indigenous oral bacteria: predominantly gram-negative anaerobic rods in a biofilm. "Anytime anybody ever asks you, what causes periodontal disease? The answer is bacteria and plaque. You find that answer on your multiple choice test question and you circle it." In class he put it more bluntly: "Don't even look at the other answers because they're wrong." Smoking and diabetes can compound it, but without bacteria there is no attachment or bone loss. Because it is a bacterial infection, antibiotics are justified, but only in selected cases.

Perio treatment, like restorative treatment, has phases. Phase I is non-surgical: oral hygiene instructions first (30-45 minutes in his office, and "arguably the most important appointment that the patient will have," because nothing works long-term if the patient can't keep their teeth clean), then scaling and root planing, then, if needed, chemotherapeutic agents, chemical substances that provide a clinical therapeutic benefit (Carranza). Antibiotics fall here: if used at all, they are used in Phase I after scaling and root planing.

When to consider antibiotics: an acute periodontal infection with systemic manifestations (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy: a localized infection starting to spread); aggressive periodontitis, which hits young patients with severe attachment and bone loss in a short time and has to be treated aggressively; and refractory periodontitis, where a patient who has done everything asked (good home care, thorough SRP, surgery, 3-month maintenance) still loses attachment. And always as an adjunct to surgical and non-surgical therapy: "the use of systemic or locally delivered antibiotics is not to be used as a monotherapy in the treatment of periodontal disease." That was his main take-home message.

Why antibiotics alone don't work: biofilms

The putative pathogens live in a biofilm, an aggregation of multiple microorganisms: if one microbial colony is a house, a biofilm is a subdivision in a protective bubble. Biofilms are a trait of supragingival and subgingival plaque. They protect and harbor the resident bacteria, let colonies survive harsh environments, and are insoluble, which makes them hard to remove: rinsing, water irrigation and mouthwashes leave them in place, like a dirty pot left soaking overnight that still has to be scrubbed. That is mechanical debridement: the patient's toothbrush and floss, and our curettes and ultrasonics. Some biofilm organisms survive antibiotic concentrations 500-1000 times greater than systemic delivery can reach. In class he called this the point to "star" and "know for life": the only way to get rid of a biofilm is mechanical debridement. A mouthrinse can supplement it, never replace it.

Biofilms make bacteria resistant to antibiotics in three ways: (1) a physical barrier that makes antibiotic penetration difficult; (2) an increased concentration of beta-lactamase inside, which destroys the beta-lactam ring of our strongest antibiotics ("anytime you see -ase on the end of a word, that's what it destroys"); and (3) a slower growth rate of the resident bacteria, which makes them less susceptible to many antibiotics.

A systemic antibiotic enters the bloodstream and spreads evenly from head to toe ("it's not a heat-seeking missile"), then diffuses into the periodontal connective tissue, junctional epithelium and crevicular region and into the gingival crevicular fluid. But the concentration there is inadequate to kill the organisms in a biofilm without mechanical debridement. Debride first, then add the antibiotic.

Bactericidal or bacteriostatic

Bacteriostatic agents inhibit the growth and reproduction of bacteria without killing them, so the body can finish the job. Bactericidal agents kill bacteria directly, but only bacteria that are actively dividing, a narrow window. That is why a biofilm's slower growth hurts our strongest antibiotics. It is also why, when two antibiotics are given at the same time, they must be both bactericidal or both bacteriostatic, never one of each: the bacteriostatic drug slows growth and shuts the bactericidal drug's only window. Antibiotics are classified by molecular structure and mechanism: they interrupt the synthesis of structural components or alter metabolic functions unique to microbial cells.

Amoxicillin, and how to write a prescription

Amoxicillin: a semisynthetic penicillin effective against gram-negative and gram-positive organisms; bactericidal by inhibiting cell wall synthesis; extended spectrum, covering many periodontal pathogens; useful in localized and generalized aggressive periodontitis. It contains a beta-lactam ring, so beta-lactamase-producing bacteria (including many periodontal pathogens) can inactivate it. Dose: 500 mg, one po tid for 7 days. Some write 875 mg bid: fewer doses a day, better compliance, and a drug only works if the patient takes it.

Abbreviations: po = by mouth; qd = once a day; bid = twice; tid = three times; qid = four times. A prescription must include the medication and strength (amoxicillin 500 mg), the quantity or volume to dispense (21 tablets for one tid for 7 days), and the instructions for use (Sig: 1 tab po tid). Also the patient's name, date of birth and address, the date, your name, address and phone number, refills, and your signature.

Hypersensitivity is the most common side effect; about 10-15% of adults are reported to have an allergic response to penicillin. Before handing over any prescription, get verbal confirmation that the patient isn't allergic to it. When a patient reports an allergy, ask what reaction they have. An upset stomach is a side effect, not an allergy. Hives or difficulty breathing (the throat closing) point to a true, potentially fatal anaphylactic reaction: then don't give that drug or anything in its class.

Many organisms are now resistant to amoxicillin. Like nearly every antibiotic, it can interfere with oral contraceptives and has shown increased bleeding times in patients on Coumadin (warfarin). Antibiotics can reduce the gut flora that make vitamin K, warfarin's antagonist, so less warfarin is inactivated and its level rises. That doesn't mean you can't prescribe; it means you let the physician know and the physician decides whether to adjust. Never change a medication another clinician prescribed.

Augmentin and the cephalosporins

Augmentin combines amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, a beta-lactamase inhibitor: it "inactivates their inactivator," so the amoxicillin can work. Effective against gram-positive and more gram-negative organisms, including anaerobes; useful in aggressive or refractory periodontitis. It may cause more GI upset (so give it with food) and is significantly more expensive than other penicillins. Written as 500 or 875 mg (the amoxicillin dose); the clavulanic acid stays 125 mg either way.

Cephalosporins: beta-lactam compounds similar in structure and action to the penicillins; bactericidal by inhibiting cell wall synthesis. Grouped in generations (1st to 4th on the slide; a 5th exists) by spectrum and order of development: later generations move from mostly gram-positive toward gram-negative coverage and more resistance to beta-lactamase, so perio favors the later ones. Some evidence of increased bone penetration; may be given with food. About 10% cross-reactivity in patients allergic to penicillin: don't give one to a patient allergic to penicillin who is unsure about cephalosporins. As taught, a patient allergic to cephalosporins has a 100% chance of penicillin allergy, so move on to another class. Cephalosporins can also interfere with oral contraceptives and increase bleeding time with warfarin.

Clindamycin

A derivative of lincomycin. It reversibly binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting protein synthesis; usually bactericidal, bacteriostatic depending on drug concentration, infection site and organism. Effective against a wide range of periodontal bacteria and the usual first choice for a patient with a true allergy to penicillins and cephalosporins. Dose: 150-300 mg po tid for 7 days. Its known side effect is pseudomembranous colitis: altered gut flora let Clostridium difficile (C. diff) overgrow, which can be fatal. The condition is reported with other antibiotics too, but clindamycin "gets a bad rap" for it. Avoid it in patients with a history of colitis.

Tetracyclines

Tetracycline is a broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotic that reversibly binds the 30S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting protein synthesis; it covers gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, aerobes and anaerobes. But widespread use over decades has bred resistant strains, so its efficacy for oral infections is significantly less than the penicillins'. It may be indicated where Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans is the prominent pathogen (localized aggressive periodontitis). As a bacteriostatic drug it may negate bactericidal agents that only work on growing cells.

Adverse effects: GI upset is the most common (nausea, vomiting, sore mouth, diarrhea, abdominal distention), and a patient who feels that bad stops taking it. Prolonged clotting time (less vitamin K from gut flora). It is deposited in bone and teeth during calcification: intrinsic stain and enamel hypoplasia (pitting, cusp deformities, more caries), so avoid it in pregnancy and in children under 8. Photosensitivity: tell patients to avoid direct sun. Absorption is inhibited by divalent and trivalent cations (calcium, magnesium, iron, aluminum): no milk or dairy, iron vitamins, mineral supplements or antacids, and take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals.

The semisynthetic derivatives doxycycline (Vibramycin) and minocycline (Minocin) are absorbed more completely and disturb the gut flora less, so they cause less GI upset. Doxycycline 100 mg po once a day; minocycline 100 mg po bid. Doxycycline is also given at a sub-antimicrobial 20 mg bid for its anticollagenase effect (Periostat, below).

Macrolides

Erythromycin, azithromycin and clarithromycin bind the 50S subunit (like clindamycin), inhibit protein synthesis in gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, and are bacteriostatic and generally narrow spectrum. Azithromycin and clarithromycin are more active against anaerobes than erythromycin.

Erythromycin: aerobic gram-positive and some anaerobic coverage, but a high incidence of bacterial resistance, so it is not recommended for periodontal disease, and nearly everyone taking it gets some GI upset. Allergy is rare, but avoid it in patients allergic to another macrolide. 250-500 mg po q6h (qid).

Azithromycin, the Z-Pak: 500 mg the first day, then 250 mg on days 2-5, five days in all, easy to comply with. Food significantly decreases its absorption: give it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals.

Clarithromycin (Biaxin): well absorbed with or without food. It has caused fetal abnormalities in animals and is pregnancy category C: avoid it in pregnant women. 250-500 mg po q12h (bid). ("If there's ever an award for the best smelling antibiotic, this wins": vanilla.)

Macrolide interactions: they can raise plasma levels of, and potentiate, many drugs, including digoxin (risking digoxin toxicity), Dilantin, oral anticoagulants (warfarin), cyclosporine, midazolam, corticosteroids and theophylline. Digoxin, a positive inotrope for heart failure, has a narrow therapeutic range. His story: Van Gogh, given digoxin in an asylum, painted The Starry Night's halos around bright lights, a symptom of digoxin toxicity.

Metronidazole

Effective only against obligate anaerobes, particularly spirochetes. It reacts with bacterial DNA, inhibiting DNA replication, and is almost always bactericidal. Useful in aggressive periodontitis and ANUG (acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis). Often combined with amoxicillin to widen the spectrum, with highly effective results: both are bactericidal, so they can be given together. 250 mg tid. Food delays but doesn't reduce absorption; bacterial resistance is low.

Cautions: it increases the anticoagulant effect of warfarin (check with the physician); it may decrease the renal excretion of lithium; it is teratogenic, so avoid it in pregnancy. Tell every patient two things: their urine may turn orange-red, and alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction with an extreme headache, like Antabuse. No alcohol.

Ciprofloxacin

A fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase; bactericidal and extended spectrum. Effective against gram-negative bacteria, but anaerobes are largely resistant, and anaerobes drive periodontal attachment loss. It is most rapidly absorbed when taken 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. It may impede the metabolism of theophylline, caffeine and warfarin, and may cause a phototoxic reaction (avoid excessive sun). 500 mg po bid, alone or with metronidazole (which covers the anaerobes) for localized aggressive periodontitis. In practice it comes far down the list: after penicillins, cephalosporins, clindamycin (ruled out by colitis) and a Z-Pak that didn't sit well.

The dosing chart: "I would know this for the exam"

Asked about doses in class, he said, "I definitely would know dosing. Absolutely," and pointed to the chart at the end of his slides: "I would know this. I would know this for the exam. It's important to know." The usual adult dose and length of treatment for each regimen on it:

  • Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid (Augmentin): 250 or 500 mg tid for 10 days.
  • Amoxicillin plus metronidazole: 375 mg amoxicillin tid plus 250 mg metronidazole tid, for 7 days.
  • Clindamycin: 150-300 mg qid for 10 days.
  • Doxycycline: 100 mg bid the first day, then 100 mg a day (once, or 50 mg bid), for 10-14 days.
  • Metronidazole: 250 mg tid or qid for 10 days.
  • Minocycline: 200 mg bid the first day, then 100 mg bid, for 10-14 days.
  • Tetracycline: 250 mg qid for 14-21 days, the longest course on the chart.

The two regimens with metronidazole are not recommended for children under 16, and the tetracyclines are dosed for children only over age 8. A few doses differ from the drug-by-drug slides, so know both: the clindamycin slide gives 150-300 mg tid for 7 days, the doxycycline slide 100 mg once a day, and Augmentin is usually written as 500 or 875 mg.

Complications of systemic antibiotics

Alteration of the GI flora with GI disturbances (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea); overgrowth of opportunistic bacteria such as C. diff; decreased effectiveness of oral contraceptives; and increased bleeding time with oral anticoagulants. To help avoid them: prophylactic Lactobacillus acidophilus (yogurt or buttermilk with active cultures) and antifungal therapy (nystatin, or Diflucan 150 mg, one tablet at the start of the course, for patients prone to yeast infections).

Local drug delivery

Locally delivered antimicrobials are an adjunct to scaling and root planing, placed subgingivally at the completion of SRP, after the biofilm is disrupted. An effective agent delivers high concentrations sustained over a long time, applied directly to the infected site, which decreases or eliminates the potential for antibiotic resistance. The disadvantage, local or systemic: neither can alter the anatomical deformities (the irregular bone) left by the disease. They are not effective against tissue-invasive organisms.

Indications: localized sites that don't respond to Phase I (the textbook answer, "not a great indication"; generalized residual pockets need surgery, not a dozen expensive cartridges) and, the real indication, localized sites in an otherwise stable maintenance patient: one site that was 3 mm for years is now 5 mm and bleeding, a last attempt before surgery. Anesthetize, debride with the ultrasonic and hand instruments, then place the agent, and re-evaluate in 4-6 weeks. Not a replacement for conventional therapy, and not for aggressive periodontitis.

The three agents sold in the US:

PerioChip: 2.5 mg chlorhexidine in a gelatin matrix, 4 x 5 x 0.35 mm ("you don't need to know these dimensions"). Self-retentive on contact with moisture, inserted into the pocket at the end of SRP, biodegradable (no removal appointment). Release peaks about 2 hours after placement, then decreases over about 9 days.

Atridox: 10% doxycycline in a biodegradable polymer, in two syringes: A holds 450 mg of the Atrigel delivery system, B holds 42.5 mg of doxycycline. Couple them and mix back and forth about 1½ minutes (100 cycles). Applied into the pocket, the excess packed in with a cord-packing instrument; it hardens, then dissolves over 3-4 weeks (no removal). The patient avoids brushing, flossing and eating at the site for at least 7 days.

Arestin: 1 mg minocycline microspheres in a biodegradable polymer, in unit-dose cartridges on a handle. Bioadhesive on contact with moisture. Insert the plastic tip to the base of the pocket and inject slowly while withdrawing. No removal appointment; the minocycline keeps a therapeutic concentration for 14 days. The patient avoids brushing the site for 12 hours and flossing it for 10 days. He still uses it in his practice from time to time.

Host modulation: what it means

Dr. Litz taught this part in class. He started by taking the term apart. A host is "an organism from which a parasite obtains its nourishment": in periodontal disease, the patient who harbors the plaque. Modulation is "an alteration of function or status of something in response to a stimulus or an altered chemical or physical environment" (Taber's). So the question is: can we change the way a patient responds to the periodontal pathogens, the response that leads to attachment loss? It is taught with antibiotics because host modulation turned to drugs, antibiotics among them.

Bacteria are the key; the host response is the engine

"This is a really, really important slide." Gram-negative bacteria are required for periodontal disease to start and progress: they are the primary etiologic factor. But they are not sufficient to cause the clinical signs of attachment loss. "Know this last bullet point": it is ultimately the host response to the bacteria that mediates tissue destruction (Reddy 2003). It is largely the way our bodies fight the bacteria that makes the deep pockets and the bone loss on radiographs. He admitted that as a student he could repeat this on an exam but only understood it as a resident.

His flowchart reads left to right, like a sentence. It always begins with the microbial challenge. Once plaque builds up along the gingival margin, the body recognizes it as foreign and mounts a host immune-inflammatory response, sending cells to destroy the bacteria, as it should. But the site turns into a war zone with collateral damage: while fighting the bacteria, our cells release pro-inflammatory cytokines and prostaglandins, which drive connective tissue and bone breakdown, seen as the clinical signs of disease: deeper pockets and bone loss. A deeper pocket is a niche for more bacteria; a bigger bacterial load calls for a bigger cellular response and more cytokines, which means more breakdown: a vicious cycle.

The take-home: it always begins with bacteria. Periodontal disease is not an autoimmune disease; the body doesn't destroy itself without a stimulus. His analogy is the car in your garage. The engine (the host response) is what gets you from periodontal health to periodontal disease, but at two in the morning it won't start by itself. It sits there dormant until someone turns the key, and the key is the bacteria.

At the cellular level

"You know these next two slides, you're going to have a pretty good understanding of the way periodontal disease works." How bacteria build up: a salivary pellicle forms within minutes of a prophylaxis and is the foundation that promotes bacterial adhesion (by the time the patient pays at the front desk, the foundation is laid). The first colonizers are mostly gram-positive cocci, fed by dietary proteins in saliva. As hygiene slips, plaque along the gingival margin inflames the soft tissue, which creates the environment for the late colonizers, the orange and then the red complexes, fed by blood and GCF. Colonization is sequential, not haphazard. The bacteria live in a biofilm, which protects them and works as a simple circulatory system, bringing nutrients and removing wastes.

How the body fights back: the cascade starts with complement, a cluster of serum proteins whose primary function is to control inflammation. Complement can lyse bacterial cell membranes directly, but its main job is as a chemoattractant for phagocytes (PMNs). It also releases histamine from mast cells, which increases vascular permeability: fluid and cells leak into the tissue, and that is the edema of inflammation. Neutrophils (PMNs) are the first responders, like the paramedics at a wreck: they arrive within about 24-48 hours of a bacterial insult to remove foreign agents. If they can't keep up, macrophages arrive later. Both are good cells ("if you didn't have them, you'd be dead"), but both release cytokines, intercellular signals that regulate cellular activity, including immune function.

His one example of a cytokine is IL-1, also called osteoclast activating factor. It activates osteoclasts (bone breakdown: a "blast" builds, a "clast" destroys), stimulates collagenase (collagen breakdown: "-ase" breaks down what it's attached to) and activates PGE2. All of this releases MMPs (matrix metalloproteinases) and more PGE2, and connective tissue and bone are lost: "kind of sounds a lot like periodontal disease." Bacteria can make enzymes that break down periodontal structures directly, but the progression and severity of attachment loss is primarily mediated by the host's immune cells. The host response is perhaps the single most important determinant of disease severity, progression and even response to therapy: host-derived enzymes (MMPs) and osteoclasts upregulated by cytokines cause most of the destruction. Bacteria are essential for periodontitis but insufficient by themselves to cause it.

Host modulation therapy, and why to step lightly

Phase I therapy targets one part of the process: removing plaque reduces the bacterial load that drives the host's inflammatory response. But bacteria are never completely eliminated by scaling and root planing, especially as pockets get deeper and in furcations. Host modulation therapy (HMT) asks whether we can down-regulate the destructive aspects and up-regulate the protective aspects of the host response so that, with conventional therapy such as SRP, the balance tips toward health.

Why isn't it further along, when the cellular picture has been known for years? His caution: "You better know what you're doing before you start monkeying around with this." Turn someone's host response down too far and a seemingly innocent bacterial infection could turn serious, even lethal. "This is territory that we really, really need to step lightly."

Host modulation isn't new to medicine, which uses it for chronic progressive disorders such as arthritis and osteoporosis. It is fairly new in dentistry: introduced in the 1990s (Williams and Golub, 1990), when pharmacologic agents, antibiotics among them, were found to possibly slow periodontitis. That is why it rides along with the antibiotics lecture.

NSAIDs

NSAIDs such as aspirin and ibuprofen inhibit the formation of prostaglandins, including PGE2, which neutrophils, macrophages, fibroblasts and gingival epithelial cells make in response to bacteria. PGE2 upregulates osteoclasts and bone resorption, so blocking it is a "pretty good first step." Given daily for up to 3 years, NSAIDs slowed alveolar bone destruction, but daily dosing is necessary: one dose, or a week or two, does nothing. That is the problem, because prolonged NSAID use causes GI problems (a bad gastric ulcer can do serious damage), hemorrhage from decreased platelet aggregation, and renal or hepatic impairment. "We can't just blindly start prescribing NSAIDs" to every periodontal patient, so long-term NSAID use for host modulation hasn't developed.

Bisphosphonates

Bisphosphonates are not new drugs. They are bone-seeking agents that inhibit bone resorption by inhibiting osteoclasts, may have anticollagenase effects too, and some studies show changes in white blood cell counts. At first glance, "we just found the magic bullet." The catch is bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ): bone necrosis after an invasive dental procedure (a simple extraction or periodontal surgery counts), with some reports of it happening spontaneously. These drugs are common, given mostly to older women for osteoporosis, by mouth or in high-dose IV forms, and most complications are with the high-dose IV forms.

BRONJ is not an infection, though it can look like one: the gingiva dies back and exposes bone that becomes necrotic. Dead bone can't come back, and left exposed it will get infected, so an oral surgeon has to scrape it off. But scraping is trauma, and trauma is what causes BRONJ: a lesion the size of a dime can come back the size of a quarter or a half dollar, a vicious cycle that is very hard to treat. Stopping the drug doesn't help quickly: bisphosphonates have a very long half-life and stay in the system for years. BRONJ has largely stunted bisphosphonates as host modulation therapy: no bisphosphonate is approved for periodontal disease.

Periostat (sub-antimicrobial dose doxycycline)

Periostat is the first FDA-approved systemic (by mouth) drug for host modulation, used as an adjunct to scaling and root planing: the same rules apply, and the biofilm still has to be disrupted mechanically. It is a low, sub-antimicrobial dose of doxycycline (SDD). Doxycycline as an antibiotic is 100 mg once a day; Periostat is 20 mg twice a day (bid), a fifth of the dose. At that dose it has no antimicrobial activity (the bacteria take one look at it and leave it alone), so resistance is not evident and it can be given long-term. Its mechanism is to inhibit collagenase, particularly the collagenase made by the host's own cells such as PMNs, where most of the destruction happens. Take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal and avoid calcium-containing products. It is contraindicated with hypersensitivity to doxycycline or other tetracyclines, in pregnant or lactating women, and in children under 12.

Does it work? Many studies say yes. His example is Caton et al., 2000, a randomized, multicenter, double-blind trial. Both groups had periodontitis and got the same SRP; one then took a placebo, the other Periostat 20 mg bid, for nine months, with re-evaluations at 3, 6 and 9 months. The Periostat group had statistically significant extra pocket reduction at every visit (4-6 mm pockets: 0.95 mm with Periostat vs 0.69 mm with placebo at 9 months; 7 mm or deeper: 1.68 vs 1.2 mm) and the same pattern in attachment gain (1.03 vs 0.86 mm; 1.35 vs 1.17 mm). He said not to learn this study's numbers, just what it shows: statistically significant, but is it clinically significant? These are fractions of a millimeter. It helps where we need all the help we can get, in refractory and aggressive periodontitis. Efficacy beyond 9 months and safety beyond 12 months haven't been established, and the net changes were limited. The AAP: adjunctive therapies (systemic antibiotics, local antibiotics, Periostat) are not a substitute for mechanical debridement, meticulous home care and the other therapies that reduce the bacterial load.

In summary, controlling the bacteria remains the primary focus: the dirty pot still has to be scrubbed. Host modulation can be considered for patients with risk factors that can't be modified or aren't easily modified, such as smoking and diabetes. Compliance is mandatory: the pill is taken twice a day, and patients must hear that it replaces neither exceptional home care and plaque control nor their frequent maintenance visits. As with blood pressure or diabetes medicine, patients tend to think a pill cures everything; it helps, but it is not a magic bullet.

Conclusions

SRP alone reduces the bacterial load, inflammation and pocket depth and gains attachment. "Definitely know this one": antibiotics alone are not indicated in the treatment of periodontal disease, even though bacteria are the primary etiologic factor, and antimicrobials are not a first line of therapy. Combined with conventional therapy, they can add pocket reduction, less inflammation and attachment gain. Use them in selected cases (aggressive periodontitis, refractory periodontitis, areas of limited involvement in maintenance patients), and aim to remove the cause of attachment loss rather than treat the symptoms. His three references: the Lexi-Comp Drug Information Handbook for Dentistry (updated every year, with each drug's dental implications; one for the office), Epocrates (a free app, constantly updated, with every drug's dosing, mechanism and side effects; "everybody in this room should have this by the end of the day"), and the Little Dental Drug Booklet (about $20 and thin enough for the clinic, with common dental prescriptions written out to copy).
full.perio-plastic-esthetics:
Dr. Abou-Arraj split this session in two. He recorded the first part (posted Nov 9): the periodontal phenotype, recession and how it is grafted, the lack of keratinized gingiva and the frenum. "The remaining two mucogingival deformities," gingival excess and abnormal color, he covers "when we meet live this week." Until a capture of that class is posted, those sections come from his 2026 slides and the class exam-review guide, and they say so.

The tissues: gingiva, alveolar mucosa and the MGJ

The mucogingival junction (MGJ) separates the gingiva from the alveolar mucosa. You can often see it, but it is found "most accurately" clinically, with a probe. All the gingiva coronal to the MGJ is keratinized gingiva. Part of it is attached, to the root surface and the bone; the rest is free gingiva, the part a probe slips under to measure the probing depth. The line between free and attached gingiva isn't visible clinically.

Mucogingival deformities

Periodontal plastic therapy treats mucogingival deformities: "any deviation from the norm" in the volume, dimension, contour or shape of the soft tissue around teeth. The 2017 World Workshop classification (Journal of Periodontology, 2018) lists seven, and the slides walk through them in order: (1) the periodontal phenotype (thin scalloped, thick scalloped, thick flat); (2) gingival or soft tissue recession, described by surface (facial or lingual, interproximal or papillary), severity (Cairo RT1, 2, 3), gingival thickness and width, any NCCL or cervical caries, the patient's esthetic concern and hypersensitivity; (3) lack of keratinized gingiva; (4) decreased vestibular depth; (5) aberrant frenum or muscle position; (6) gingival excess (pseudopocket, inconsistent gingival margin, excessive gingival display, gingival enlargement); and (7) abnormal color (a mucogingival tattoo).

The periodontal phenotype

The phenotype has two parts: the tissue's thickness, thin or thick, and the gingival line's contour, scalloped or flat. Thin tissue can be judged by eye (you can almost see the roots through it), but the validated way is the probe: slide it into the sulcus. If you can see the probe through the tissue, the phenotype is thin, 1 mm or less. If you can't see it, the phenotype is thick, more than 1 mm.

Why it matters: a thin phenotype is predisposed to recession, and recession that is already there tends to progress on it, while a thick phenotype resists it. His example: a young patient about to start orthodontics had a thin phenotype over his incisors, so thin you could see the roots. Orthodontic movement, then years of toothbrushing on top of it, would put him at risk of recession he didn't have yet. So before the orthodontics the phenotype was changed from thin to thick: a trapezoidal, full-thickness flap, a connective tissue graft from the palate sutured over the two central incisors (the teeth most at risk), and the flap put back over the graft to cover it completely. At two weeks the tissue was already thicker, and he was cleared for orthodontics with less risk of recession.

Recession: what it is and who gets it

Recession is "the location of the marginal periodontal tissues apical to the cemento-enamel junction" (AAP Glossary, 2001): part of the root is exposed. Measure it with the probe from the gingival margin to the CEJ, at the same six sites as probing depth, so it can be recorded and followed over time. It isn't only on the straight facial or lingual: note any interproximal recession too, because it "could change totally the prognosis of the treatment."

It is common. The slide (Albandar and Kingman, 1999): 88% of people 65 and older and 50% of people 18 to 64 have at least one site with recession, and prevalence and extent rise significantly with age. In the recording he put it another way: more than half of the US population 30 or older has at least 1 mm of recession, and almost a quarter has at least one tooth surface with 3 mm or more. Older people have more not because of their age but because they have accumulated risk factors over more years. Recession is more common in men than in women and in African-Americans than in other groups, and most common on the buccal surfaces of maxillary molars (first molars in particular) and mandibular central incisors; canines are also commonly affected.

Predisposing factors

The slide lists ten: periodontal disease (periodontitis); trauma (toothbrushing, flossing, self-inflicted, foreign objects); anatomic variations (fenestration, dehiscence and abnormal tooth position); lack of keratinized gingiva; a thin gingival phenotype; orthodontic treatment; previous periodontal surgery; a high muscle attachment and aberrant frenum; iatrogenic factors related to the location of restoration margins; and the use of smokeless tobacco. What he added in the recording:

Periodontitis, not gingivitis: attachment and bone loss expose the root. Previous periodontal surgery: after Phase I and resective Phase II therapy, "we caused most of this recession," on purpose, to leave an environment without pockets that the patient can keep clean. Toothbrushing is the most common traumatic factor: hard bristles, or an aggressive brusher whatever the bristle. The trauma list also takes in flossing habits, self-inflicted oral habits, foreign objects (a fingernail, a pen) and caustic medicaments applied directly to the gingiva.

Anatomic variations. A fenestration is a window in the bone over the root; a dehiscence is missing facial bone from the crest apically. A tooth positioned buccally on the arch has thinner facial tissue and takes more of the toothbrush. Moving it back onto the arch orthodontically, into its alveolar housing, can resolve some of the recession, at least partly, without a graft. Put a dehiscence or fenestration together with a thin phenotype and an aggressive brusher, and you have "the perfect storm."

Orthodontic treatment: pushing teeth buccally out of the alveolar housing (proclining incisors) over a thin phenotype can cause recession. Some studies find incisor proclination doesn't; he calls it controversial and advises caution about when to propose grafting. Iatrogenic margins: an intrasulcular or subgingival crown margin on a thin phenotype, an ill-fitting margin or an overcontoured restoration can lead to recession (which doesn't mean every crown needs a graft). A high frenum or muscle attachment pulls on the margin with every movement. Smokeless tobacco, held in one spot, usually the lower premolar or molar area, changes the tissue locally and can cause a severe localized recession. His worst case had no pockets and no interproximal bone loss, but recessions reaching the bottom of the vestibule, hard to treat even with several attempts.

How recession develops

Two mechanisms (from Zucchelli's textbook). Toothbrushing trauma, especially on thin tissue: the epithelium is abraded, the connective tissue under it responds with inflammation, an ulcer forms at the surface, and with continued trauma the margin recedes. Plaque-related: the same process as periodontitis (plaque in the sulcus with poor hygiene, apical and lateral migration of the junctional epithelium, loss of attachment), here on a local scale on a thin phenotype. "The key word here is inflammation": it is what actually causes recession, and the factors above are predisposing factors that make it happen.

The Cairo classification: how much root can you cover?

Before proposing a graft, assess how severe the recession is and what treatment can achieve. The Cairo classification (2011) has three types, read from the interproximal attachment:
