RT1: recession with no loss of interproximal attachment; the interproximal CEJ can't be detected clinically on the mesial or the distal. The best prognosis: about 100% root coverage is achievable.

RT2: recession with loss of interproximal attachment, where the interproximal CAL (from the interproximal CEJ to the depth of the interproximal sulcus or pocket) is less than or equal to the buccal CAL (from the buccal CEJ to the depth of the buccal sulcus or pocket). You can see the CEJ interproximally. Expect partial root coverage, about 50 to 60% in cases like his: at best up to the level of the interproximal attachment on either side. The tissue can't be pulled any higher, because there is no framework and no blood supply interproximally to hold it there ("if we know how to fix this, we could ... cure everybody from periodontitis").

RT3: loss of interproximal attachment where the interproximal CAL is greater than the buccal CAL. A graft for root coverage "would not end up achieving that root coverage at all," so root coverage isn't encouraged. The classification is how you decide when to propose a soft tissue graft for root coverage, and when not to.

Why treat recession

Exposed roots and lost tissue raise the likelihood of (1) dentinal hypersensitivity, (2) soft tissue discomfort (thin tissue with little keratinized gingiva can hurt to brush), (3) root surface caries, (4) esthetic concerns, (5) interference with adequate mechanical plaque control, and (6) greater susceptibility to inflammatory insult. And recession doesn't sit still: a systematic review (Chambrone and Tatakis, 2016) found that untreated recession defects continue to progress, the margin moving further apical. So "let's just monitor it" because it doesn't hurt, isn't sensitive and isn't in the esthetic zone doesn't mean it will stay the same. Apart from RT3, recession should be considered for treatment when indicated. (Restorative ways to treat recession are for next year's course; this session is about soft tissue grafting.)

Soft tissue grafts: where they come from

The two main sources in the US are the patient's own tissue, an autograft, and donor tissue from a tissue bank, an allograft; there are others (bovine, porcine). The most common graft comes from the palate (or the tuberosity), because the palate is orthokeratinized: its tissue "carries that information of keratinization with it" to the recipient site. Palatal connective tissue induces epithelial differentiation and keratinization. From the palate you take either a free gingival graft (FGG), the epithelium together with the lamina propria (the connective tissue) under it in one piece, or a subepithelial connective tissue graft (SCTG, or CTG), the connective tissue without the epithelium.

The palate's layers, from the surface in: the epithelium (0.3-0.6 mm, thin), the lamina propria (connective tissue, 1.25-3.0 mm, usually the thickest), the submucosa (adipose and glandular tissue), then bone. An epithelialized graft is thin at 0.5-0.8 mm, average at 0.9-1.4 mm and thick at 1.5-2.0 mm or more. A thick graft brings much of the fat layer with it, and that is usually removed so it doesn't slow the healing.

The anatomy to stay away from is the greater palatine artery and nerve, the neurovascular bundle. On the slide it runs about 7 mm from the CEJ in a shallow palate, 12 mm in an average palate and 17 mm in a high palate. So a high, deep palatal vault gives the most room for error when harvesting (the exam-review guide's point). There are guidelines for which area to harvest from (premolar, molar) and how far up the palate to go.

Two ways to harvest a CTG: a trap door, elevating the epithelium and connective tissue together and then taking the connective tissue from under the epithelium; or harvesting the whole rectangle with its epithelium, like an FGG, and removing the epithelium afterwards. The exam-review guide puts it this way: sometimes an FGG is harvested but delivered as a CTG, because that is easier to harvest and heal.

The rule for which graft: if the graft will be covered by a flap, it must be connective tissue only. The inner side of the flap is connective tissue, and epithelium placed against it "just would not heal properly." If the graft will be left exposed, not covered by the flap, use an FGG, with its epithelium.

Root coverage with a CTG and a coronally advanced flap

His case: recession on #10 and #11 (part of a composite filling was removed first). A trapezoidal flap, raised partial thickness to keep some of the periosteum, exposed the roots; the graft size was planned (a template helps) and a CTG harvested from the palate, its epithelium removed. The graft was placed and sutured, then the flap was advanced coronally over it, tension free, so it holds its coronal position covering the recessions and the graft completely. At about four weeks the coverage was good, and coverage that looks like this early usually holds. The profile view shows the other gain: much thicker tissue over the roots, a thick phenotype "that by definition would resist much better" further recession. "We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft."

Many teeth: the acellular dermal matrix allograft

Treating many teeth from the palate means a large, invasive harvest. When you can avoid that, use a soft tissue allograft: donated human dermis, usually from cadavers, processed to remove the epidermis, the hair follicles and the existing cells. What is left, the acellular dermal matrix (ADM, or ADMA; AlloDerm is one), is a matrix of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers with no cells. It wasn't designed for dentistry: it has been used since 1995 for burns, head and neck reconstruction, urology (bladder slings, pelvic floor reconstruction), orthopedics (rotator cuff repair, periosteal replacement) and hernia repair, and in dentistry since 1997, now in dental sizes. It is the most common soft tissue allograft (exam-review guide).

Advantages (slide): it eliminates the need for a donor site; increases patient acceptance (no surgery on the roof of the mouth); decreases surgical time; treats multiple defects in one procedure ("quote-unquote unlimited quantities"); achieves esthetic results comparable or superior to autogenous tissue; and is easy to use. Disadvantages (recording): it is "more or less a dead piece of skin" with nothing to contribute to the healing, "like a band-aid." So it must be fully covered by the flap, because it heals poorly left exposed without a blood supply. Over time it is remodeled and replaced by the patient's own tissue (histology shows this). In a more demanding site it can't give the same benefit as autogenous tissue; the exam-review guide's summary is that allografts don't work as well as autografts but have many advantages.

His case: canine to canine, five or six teeth, with a combination of RT2 and RT3 recessions. The flap was a tunnel (pouch): like an envelope flap but without raising the papillae, going into the sulcus of each tooth and connecting sulcus to sulcus into one plane under the tissue. The ADM went through two water baths, the second with tetracycline, was snaked into the tunnel over the roots, held with sling sutures, and the flap was advanced coronally to cover it completely. At six months, given the RT2 and RT3 start, the result was considered quite successful.

Lack of keratinized gingiva

Keratinized gingiva (KG) runs from the gingival margin to the MGJ, and it can be thin or thick. Besides the color change (pink gingiva, redder mucosa), find the MGJ by rolling the probe, held horizontally, from the mucosa toward the margin: the loose, mobile mucosa rolls with it, and at the MGJ the tissue stops rolling. From there to the gingival margin is the width of keratinized gingiva. It can be measured on edentulous ridges too.

On average (Lindhe's figure), the maxillary facial KG is widest at the incisors, narrowest at the canine and first premolar, and wider again toward the molars, and the mandible follows a similar pattern; on the mandibular lingual it is narrowest at the incisors and widens toward the molars. Patients vary.

Is keratinized gingiva needed? A zone of attached gingiva is, of and by itself, not essential for keeping periodontal health and attachment, when dental plaque is controlled and there are no other traumatic factors (Kennedy and colleagues, 1985; Scheyer and colleagues, the AAP Regeneration Workshop, 2015). If plaque control is suboptimal, at least 2 mm of KG is needed to prevent attachment loss. Many patients don't have optimal plaque control, so a tooth with less than 2 mm of KG is likely prone to recession. That doesn't mean every such tooth needs a graft: it is case by case. Not every patient lacking KG has recession, but lacking it predisposes to it, while a thick phenotype with a wide band of KG resists it.

Gaining keratinized gingiva: an FGG left exposed

His patient had an RT2 recession on a sensitive tooth with no KG: the site was a plaque trap, chronically irritating the margin and leading to more recession. The goal was to change the quality of the tissue, creating a band of KG; root coverage would be a bonus. A CTG under a coronally advanced flap wouldn't do it: covering the graft with the only tissue there, alveolar mucosa, gains no keratinized gingiva, because mucosa doesn't become keratinized just because it covers a graft. So he used a free gingival graft with an apically positioned flap: a trapezoidal flap (a horizontal incision and two vertical ones) placed apically, and an FGG from the palate, with its epithelium, left exposed so it heals into a band of KG, bringing its own determination to keratinize. Covering it with the flap would deny it that. The palate heals by secondary intention. The graft is held only by sutures, so patients are told not to pull the lip down to look at it every day, to keep a soft diet and not to brush the area while it heals. At three months there was a good band of KG where there had been none, blending with the neighboring tissue (bigger on the apical side), and partial root coverage, as expected for RT2. Her sensitivity was gone, the site was easier to clean and less of a plaque trap, and the phenotype was thicker and more protective.

The frenum and the vestibule

A highly attached frenum can be a critical factor in the progression of recession: with the lip and every muscle movement in the area (not only when someone pulls the lip), it pulls on the gingival margin, which facilitates plaque accumulation and adds to the recession. In one patient, pulling the lip pulled all the way to the margin of a central incisor with no KG. In another, the frenum stood in the way of the esthetic result while her crowns were being redone (the provisionals had closed the black triangle), so a frenectomy was done before the final restorations. It is a quick, easy procedure: dissect around the frenum, excise the tissue that forms it in a diamond shape, and close the diamond with a few sutures that extend into the lip. The classification lists decreased vestibular depth beside it, and the slides show both together.

Gingival excess (slides; the live session)

The slides give four etiologies of gingival excess, each with its treatment. 1. Pseudopocket: gingivitis, the gingiva swollen coronally so the probing depth grows without attachment loss. Treatment: improved oral hygiene measures and scaling. 2. Gingival enlargement: gingival diseases modified by medications, phenytoin, calcium channel blockers and cyclosporine. Treatment: gingivectomy, improved oral hygiene and possibly a change of the contributing medication. 3. Inconsistent gingival margins: discrepant gingival margins of contralateral teeth, a gingival line discrepancy. Treatment: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap. 4. Excessive gingival display, a "gummy smile." Treatment: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap, but first find its cause, because it has several.

Excessive gingival display: find the cause

The possible etiologies, each with the finding that points to it on the slides: short clinical crowns (altered passive eruption), with abnormal tooth dimensions and proportions and gingival line asymmetries; vertical maxillary excess, with an increased lower facial third; a short upper lip, with a lip length under 20 mm; a hypermobile upper lip, with lip mobility over 8 mm; or a combination of these.

Passive eruption and altered passive eruption

In passive eruption the gingival complex migrates in the apical direction, gradually exposing the crown, until the dentogingival junction settles in a final stable position at the cervical level (Alpiste-Illueca). In altered passive eruption it doesn't, and the teeth look short: the clinical crown is shorter than the anatomical crown. Coslet's classification reads it on two axes. Type 1: a wider gingival dimension from the free gingival margin to the MGJ, with the MGJ apical to the alveolar crest. Type 2: a normal dimension, with the MGJ at the level of the CEJ. Subcategory A: more than 1 mm between the CEJ and the osseous crest. Subcategory B: the osseous crest in close proximity to the CEJ. Types 1A and 1B are the most frequently encountered.

The treatment is crown lengthening, matched to the type: a gingivectomy only in Type 1A; an apically positioned flap in Type 2A; an apically positioned flap plus osseous surgery in Types 1B and 2B. The logic behind the rule: in a B type the bone itself sits too close to the CEJ, so the bone has to be moved, whatever the gingiva; in Type 2 the band of gingiva is only of normal width, so cutting gingiva away would cost keratinized gingiva, and the flap moves the band apically instead. Only Type 1A has both extra gingiva and room above the bone.

Crown lengthening: the pretreatment evaluation

Crown lengthening works on the difference between the clinical crown, what shows above the gingiva, and the anatomical crown, the enamel down to the CEJ. Before it, check the clinical parameters, probing depth, gingival health and the width of keratinized gingiva, and the radiographic parameters: the apical extent of any fracture or caries, root length and form, the level of the alveolar crest, and pulpal involvement (Abou-Arraj and Souccar, 2013).

The esthetic evaluation

His checklist on the slides. Facial symmetry: the facial thirds, and the facial midline against the dental midline; an increased lower facial third suggests vertical maxillary excess. Smile line (lip line): high, medium or low. Incisal line: it should be consonant with the lower lip. Upper lip, height and mobility: 20-22 mm for women, 22-24 mm for men, and normal lip mobility is 6-8 mm, measured with a caliper at rest and in a full smile. Gingival line: the central incisors and canines at the same level, and the lateral incisors 1 mm coronal to them. Tooth shape, dimensions and proportions: the golden proportion, which the slides show in nature, art and architecture. Seen from the front, the central incisor is about 1.618 times as wide as the lateral, and the lateral 1.618 times the visible part of the canine, so centrals, laterals and canines show at about 1.618 : 1 : 0.618 (the exam-review guide rounds it to 1.6, 1 and 0.6 for half the canine). On the slide a 9 mm central goes with a 5.56 mm lateral and 3.44 mm of canine.

Treating excessive gingival display

The slide's table: altered passive eruption, crown lengthening and restorative therapy; vertical maxillary excess, orthodontics and orthognathic surgery, and periodontics may be required to correct the gingival display; a hypermobile upper lip, lip repositioning surgery or Botox may reduce the display; a short upper lip, no good options. When several factors are present, a combination of therapies may be considered.

Patient 1

A healthy 28-year-old woman: "I don't like the color of my front teeth" (generalized fluorosis). She declined orthodontics and wanted veneers. The esthetic evaluation: equal facial thirds; the dental midline slightly to the right; a high lip line at full smile; normal upper lip length and mobility; canted gingival and incisal lines, the incisal line not consonant with the lower lip; flat gingival heights of contour on #8, 9 and 10, with the margins of #7 and #10 more apical than those of #6, 8 and 9, a discrepancy across all the anterior teeth; and square teeth #8, 9 and 10 (the centrals 8 mm wide and 8.5-9 mm high, the laterals 6 mm wide and 7.5-8 mm high). With normal facial thirds and a normal lip, the gummy smile came from the teeth and gingiva, short clinical crowns and an uneven gingival line, so the plan was crown lengthening, then the veneers. The photos follow her from the planned gingival line on the cast, through the surgery, to the veneers, with healing at 1 week, 3 weeks, 6 months and 18 months.

Abnormal color: the mucogingival tattoo

The last deformity in the classification (slides; the live session): a gray discoloration of the gingiva or mucosa, a mucogingival tattoo. The slides show one case: the stained tissue over an anterior bridge was removed, a graft harvested from the palate was sutured in its place, and the area was recontoured with a gingivoplasty 3 months after the grafting.

plain.diagnosis-tx-planning:
Every gum-disease diagnosis starts with three measurements. Probing depth (PD) is how far the probe sinks: from the edge of the gum (the gingival margin) down to the bottom of the pocket. Recession (GR) is how far the gum has pulled back: from the CEJ (the line where enamel meets root) to the gum edge. Clinical attachment level (CAL) is the one that counts for staging. It is the two added together, which works out to the distance from the CEJ down to the bottom of the pocket. It tells you how much of the tooth's real attachment has been lost.

The sign matters. If the gum edge sits above the CEJ (so you can't see any root), recession is written as a negative number and CAL comes out smaller than the probing depth. If root is showing, recession is positive and CAL comes out bigger than the probing depth. Example: a 7 mm pocket with the CEJ hiding 4 mm under the gum is only 3 mm of attachment loss. A shallow 2 mm pocket with 4 mm of root showing is 6 mm of attachment loss. The second tooth looks worse on paper, but it is easier to keep, because the patient can actually reach a 2 mm pocket with a brush.

X-rays show what a probe can't reach. Use periapicals plus vertical bitewings, not horizontal ones. A horizontal bitewing can miss the bone loss in one of the two jaws completely. A panoramic is a good overview, but it isn't detailed enough to diagnose gum disease by itself.

Health, gingivitis, or periodontitis

Health: no pocket deeper than 3 mm, no bleeding, no lost attachment, no lost bone. Gingivitis (inflamed gums from plaque) can have 4-5 mm pockets that bleed, but there is no attachment loss and no bone loss. The problem is only in the gums, and it goes away completely once the plaque is controlled. Before calling a mouth "gingivitis," at least 10% of sites should bleed. Probing pressure varies between people, so two or three bleeding spots on their own shouldn't decide it.

Periodontitis is different: attachment loss and bone loss are both there, pockets often reach 6 mm or more, and it does not fully reverse. Treatment can stop it, but the best result is healthy gums on a reduced periodontium (less support than the patient started with), not a return to the original attachment.

"Intact" or "reduced" describes how much support is left, separately from whether there is disease right now. An intact periodontium can be healthy or have gingivitis. A reduced one (after old periodontitis, crown lengthening, or plain recession) can also be healthy or inflamed. A treated periodontitis patient who stays stable on maintenance is called healthy on a reduced periodontium. You don't re-stage them unless the disease comes back. If pockets deepen and bleeding returns at a later visit, the diagnosis moves back toward periodontitis, depending on how widespread it is.

Recession is a sign, not a diagnosis

Gums can recede in people who have never had periodontitis, so recession gets its own grading, based on how much attachment is also lost between the teeth. RT1: no loss between the teeth, so the root can be fully covered with surgery. RT2: some loss between the teeth, but less than on the cheek side, so only partial coverage is expected. RT3: more loss between the teeth than on the cheek side, so root coverage isn't tried, because it won't work.

Staging and grading

Staging answers "how bad is it, and how hard will it be to treat?" The best measure is CAL between the teeth; bone loss on the X-ray is the backup. Stages 1 and 2 are early: more attachment loss, but bone loss still in the top third of the root. Stages 3 and 4 both have CAL of 5 mm or more and bone loss into the middle third or deeper. What separates 3 from 4 is not more attachment loss. It is how many teeth were lost to gum disease (4 or fewer is Stage 3, 5 or more is Stage 4) and whether the case needs complex, multi-specialty rebuilding.

Three findings jump a case straight to Stage 3 or 4 no matter what the CAL says: vertical (angular) bone loss of 3 mm or more, a Class II or III furcation (bone loss between the roots), and any tooth lost to periodontitis. A common trap: deep pockets alone never prove periodontitis. Without confirmed bone loss, a mouth full of 4s and 5s could just be widespread gingivitis.

Grading answers "how fast is it moving, and how will this patient respond?" Start by assuming Grade B (moderate) and move only if the evidence says so. If old records show change over time, that is the best evidence. If not, take the percent bone loss on the worst tooth and divide by the patient's age: under 0.25 points to Grade A, 0.25 to 1.0 to Grade B, over 1.0 to Grade C. Two things can only push the grade up: heavy smoking (more than 10 cigarettes a day) and an HbA1c of 7% or higher. Either one makes it Grade C even if the ratio says B. Not smoking or not having diabetes never earns a lower grade. Each patient gets one stage (from the single worst site) and one grade.

Reading a bone defect

When the gum is lifted during surgery, a bone defect is described by how many bony walls are still standing around the damaged root. Picture standing inside the hole and counting the walls around you. A 3-wall defect (cheek side, tongue side, and the wall facing the next tooth are still there; only the root itself is bare) has the best chance of growing bone back. A 2-wall defect has lost one of those walls. When the bone is gone on both sides between the teeth and only the cheek and tongue walls are left, that shape is called a crater. A 1-wall defect has the worst chance. X-rays can fool you here: thick outer bone, especially on the lower jaw, can hide a defect you only see once the gum is lifted.

From diagnosis to treatment plan

Everyone starts with Phase I (non-surgical care), whatever the stage: hygiene coaching, scaling and root planing (a deep cleaning of the roots), help quitting smoking, fixing fillings or crowns whose edges trap plaque, and cavity treatment. Cavities are easy to forget, but they belong in Phase I, before or alongside the deep cleaning, because a broken-down surface is harder to clean. Permanent crowns or a final partial denture wait until gum treatment is finished; a temporary crown fills the gap.

The decision about surgery (Phase II) is made at the Phase I re-evaluation visit, not at the first exam, because that is when you can see how well the gums healed and how well the patient kept up at home. Stage 1-2 cases often clear up with Phase I alone and go straight to maintenance. Stage 3-4 cases more often need surgery: either reshaping bone so it is easy to keep clean (resective surgery) or regrowing bone in a good-shaped defect (regenerative surgery). Every plan ends in maintenance, and the evidence for it is clear: people who refuse treatment lose about three times as many teeth as treated people, and treated people who skip maintenance lose teeth about twice as fast as those who keep their recall visits.
plain.incisions-flaps-sutures:
Gum surgeries sit on a scale. A simple extraction may need no cut and no flap at all. A graft over a receded root needs a small flap lifted just a little. A sinus lift or ridge graft needs a big flap opened with several cuts. Which cut and flap to use is partly a matter of the surgeon's preference (Dr. Basma said two surgeons can disagree on the same case), but a small set of designs covers almost everything.

Naming an incision: it's about the tooth, not the technique

The most-missed point in this session: intrasulcular and crestal are the same cut. Only the name changes, depending on whether a tooth is there. With a tooth present, the blade goes into the sulcus (the small gap between gum and tooth) and separates the gum fibers from the tooth all the way around: cheek side, tongue side, and through the papillae (the gum points between teeth). That is intrasulcular. Where there is no tooth, there's no sulcus, so the same straight cut along the top of the ridge is called crestal. Including more teeth in this cut gives a bigger flap and more room to work, but including teeth you don't need hurts the look of the result for no gain.

When that cut alone doesn't open enough room (most big bone grafts), you add a vertical releasing incision at the line angle of a tooth (the corner where the front surface turns into the side surface). It opens a bigger flap without adding more teeth to the horizontal cut. One vertical plus an intrasulcular cut across three teeth (for example, distal of #7 with the sulcus cut on 7, 8 and 9) makes a triangle-shaped pyramidal flap, which is enough for an implant with a small bone graft on top. Two verticals, one on each side, make a trapezoidal flap. That is needed for large vertical bone grafts, because two releases let the flap slide up and close over the graft without tension. One vertical usually can't stretch that far without tearing.

One more design barely lifts anything: the envelope (pouch) flap. The papillae are never touched. Only the cheek-side gum is loosened, just enough to slide it up over a gum graft (from the patient or a donor), leaving the gum between the teeth completely intact. It is the go-to design for covering exposed roots, where disturbing the papilla would work against the cosmetic goal.

Reading a flap design

Besides how it is opened, a flap is described three more ways. Thickness: full-thickness lifts the periosteum (the thin skin over the bone) with the flap and bares the bone; split-thickness leaves the periosteum on the bone. Where it goes back: moved up past the CEJ to cover roots, or moved down for crown lengthening and bone reshaping. Papilla: kept intact or not. A sulcular flap (sulcus cut only, no vertical) gives the least room and is hard to move because the tissue stays attached at the sides. It is the smallest option, used for small grafts or a single implant. Adding one more tooth on each side (still no vertical) buys a bit more room without a releasing cut.

Full vs. split has a simple rule: if the surgery involves bone in any way, go full thickness and expose it. If it's only about soft tissue, go split thickness and leave the periosteum behind as a living bed. That covers every case in the course. Implants, bone, ridge and sinus grafts, crown lengthening and bone reshaping are all full thickness. Gum grafting is the one split-thickness exception, because the graft needs that blood-rich bed to connect its blood vessels to the patient's.

A fourth incision: sub-marginal, for eliminating a pocket

The in-class review added a fourth cut that works differently from the others: the sub-marginal incision. "Sub" means below: it is made below the gum edge, not in the sulcus or on the ridge. The other cuts are for access and get closed back where they were. This one removes tissue on purpose: it is scalloped through the pocket wall and the gum above it is cut away, not lifted and put back. The goal is getting rid of a deep pocket during bone surgery. If a site probes 6 mm where 3 mm is normal, trimming about 3 mm of pocket wall leaves a shallow, cleanable sulcus instead of a deep pocket that keeps refilling with bacteria between visits.

The catch is deliberate: this cut creates recession (the gum edge ends up lower on the tooth after healing). That is the right trade when the alternative is a pocket the patient can't keep clean. It is the wrong call, and never done, on a site being treated for recession. The question is always what the real problem is: a deep pocket calls for a sub-marginal cut; thin or receded gum calls for a graft. They aren't contradictory, just answers to different problems.

Choosing a suture material

Stitches come in two big groups. Absorbable ones dissolve in the body on their own (gut, chromic gut, and synthetics like Vicryl and Monocryl). Non-absorbable ones have to be taken out, usually at 10-14 days, or are left long-term (silk, ePTFE, polypropylene/Prolene, nylon). Plain gut dissolves fastest (7-10 days). Chromic gut is treated with chromium salts and lasts a bit longer (10-14 days). Synthetics like Vicryl keep their strength for 2-3 weeks and dissolve over a longer time. Absorbables make sense for quick cases in kids or simple extractions, where a removal visit is a hassle. Non-absorbables like ePTFE are preferred over big bone grafts because they attract less plaque, are strong, and won't break down too early.

The course chart compares six materials by natural vs. synthetic, single-strand vs. braided, how fast they dissolve, strength, how much they irritate tissue, and how they handle (full chart in Review). Chromic gut: natural, single strand, dissolves fastest (7-10 days), handles very badly. Used at extraction sites, implants without extra grafting, or to hold a collagen membrane. The two synthetic dissolvers differ by build. PGA is braided, dissolves slowest (55-70 days), handles beautifully, but irritates tissue, which fits ridge and sinus grafts that heal slowly. PGCL is a single strand, dissolves faster (22-55 days) and is gentler on tissue, which fits gum grafts and cosmetic crown lengthening. Of the ones that must be removed: polypropylene behaves like nylon and doesn't stick to tissue; silk handles beautifully but irritates tissue the most of anything on the list and comes out at 7 days; PTFE costs the most and is used for nearly every surgery except pure gum grafts.

Single strand vs. braided isn't just about feel; it's about infection. A braided stitch soaks up and traps bacteria like a wick. A smooth single strand doesn't. That is exactly why silk scores so badly for irritation. If you use a braided stitch, wipe it with chlorhexidine gauze before pulling it out, so you don't drag plaque back through the wound.

Grafting from the palate: donor-site selection and protection

Keratinized gum (pale pink, firm, doesn't move) protects the tooth from the wear of chewing, the way tough skin protects you in a fall better than the thin lining inside your cheek. Non-keratinized tissue (red, thin, loose, full of blood vessels) can't take that load. When a tooth or implant doesn't have enough firm gum, you graft some, and the palate is the best source because it is all firm, keratinized, fixed tissue. Take it from the molar area, not the premolar area. The premolar area has more fat under the surface, and fat melts away after it is moved, so a graft with too much fat visibly shrinks. From the surface down, the palate is: epithelium (surface layer), then connective tissue (lamina propria), then fat over bone. A connective tissue graft keeps only the middle layer: the surface is trimmed off and the fat is avoided on purpose.

Grafts work because two raw, cut surfaces held together will join their blood vessels and heal as one, the same way two cut fingers held together can reattach, but two fingers just pressed together (skin intact) never will. That's also why the site receiving the graft is prepared split thickness: the periosteum left on the bone gives the graft a living surface to fuse to. The donor spot on the roof of the mouth is left as an open wound, and it hurts (compared in class to a bad pizza burn, since every sip and swallow touches raw nerve endings). Options to protect it: a composite stent made before the harvest to keep the palate's shape, PRF (a gel made from the patient's own blood) laid over the wound, or a custom palatal stent or night guard worn for at least three days while it heals over, taken out only to clean. Watch out for the greater palatine artery in this area; nicking it is the most common cause of serious bleeding during a palatal harvest.

The needle matters as much as the thread. A reverse cutting needle keeps its flat side toward the tissue as it comes up, so it is less likely to tear through than a regular cutting needle. A more curved needle takes a deeper bite. A thicker needle goes through more tissue but needs more wrist turn. For thread size, a bigger number means a thinner thread, and thinner thread needs more knots to hold.

Choosing a technique

Single interrupted stitches (and the figure-8 version) are the everyday default: each one is tied on its own. Horizontal mattress stitches are a must for bigger bone grafts and keep the flap edges from rolling inward, but tied too tight they choke the blood supply to the edge and can cause bone death and the wound opening up. Vertical mattress stitches pull tissue together most closely and turn the edges out; they are the choice for rebuilding papillae in the front of the mouth or closing an opening into the sinus. Continuous and continuous-locking stitches put the bites close together for a tight seal, but if one throw fails the whole line can come loose (a real risk with slippery single-strand thread), so they're kept for long toothless areas, bone smoothing and root-tip surgery. Sling and periosteal-anchor stitches finish the list: one wraps around a single tooth to reposition a flap, the other anchors the flap to the periosteum to hold it lower or to the side.

Five surgical principles

Every cut and flap in the course follows five rules: (1) one firm, continuous stroke, not several shaky ones; (2) keep the cut away from the actual defect, never right over it; (3) put vertical cuts at the line angle of the tooth; (4) lift the periosteum as part of the flap; and (5) make the base of the flap at least as wide as its free edge, because once the flap is lifted, the base is its only blood supply.

Ortho heads-up: if an orthodontist plans to push thin-gummed front teeth further forward, graft first to thicken the gum. Pushing a tooth through thin bone and gum tends to cause recession, and it's easier to prevent than to fix. The best time to treat recession is always as early as possible.
plain.risk-assessment:
Dr. Geisinger's starting point: if you treat every patient the same no matter their risk, you're set up to fail. Periodontitis isn't only an infection. It's an inflammation problem driven by the immune system, and how fast it moves (or whether it moves at all) depends on the patient, the specific site, and their environment. "One size does not fit all" is the theme. The practical question is: given what you know about this patient, how do you turn it into a recall schedule, a point where you step up treatment, and a conversation they'll act on?

The scale of the problem, and who is actually looking

About 42.5% of US adults over 30 have periodontitis (roughly 64.7 million people), rising to 70.1% of adults 65 and older. It's more common in men (56.4%) than women (38.4%), in current smokers (64.2%), in people below the poverty line (65.4%), and in people without a high school diploma (66.9%). The number that stings: 72% of patients who turn out to have periodontitis came in saying "I'm just here for my cleaning." Most have no idea. It doesn't hurt, bleeding when brushing feels normal, and nobody has measured or explained it to them. So the clinician is often the first and only person who will spot it.

Billing data shows the gap. Dentistry bills procedures, not diagnoses. A "prophy" (code D1110) is a preventive cleaning meant only for people with no gum disease and no history of it. Since gum disease gets more common with age, prophy's share of cleanings should shrink as patients get older. Instead it grows: 72.3% of cleanings at ages 19-34, 87.5% at 35-49, and 95.4% at 50-64. That's the opposite of what should happen, which suggests disease is being missed (or not treated properly) more often as patients age.

P4 (P5) medicine vs. Hippocratic medicine

Traditional (Hippocratic) medicine starts from "do no harm," which in practice tends to mean reacting: treat disease once it shows up. P4 medicine means personalized, preventive, predictive and participatory: estimate each patient's risk, tailor it to their own risk factors, and make them an active partner in their care instead of someone who just gets instructions. For gum care the lecture adds a fifth P, periodontal, and calls it P5 care.

Why is risk hard to estimate? Partly because "you get out what you put in." A bitewing that doesn't show the front teeth can hide the worst sites. A yearly panoramic-plus-bitewings routine may never picture the area that matters. In a UAB review of treated maintenance patients, over 40% of the records had to be thrown out because bleeding on probing had never been written down, and if you don't record inflammation, you can't tell how much the patient is carrying.

A full risk workup, practically

A risk workup has five parts: an interview (health history, lifestyle, whole-body conditions); a full gum exam (pocket depths, attachment levels, plaque, bleeding, pus, furcations, loose teeth, fremitus); X-rays to check bone levels; deciding whether you need the patient's physician (an HbA1c for a diabetic, an INR for someone on blood thinners); and a lifestyle check (tobacco, alcohol, stress). The American Academy of Periodontology recommends a full gum evaluation at least once a year for adults, more often for higher-risk patients, plus a quick screen at every visit.

Why now? And what a 3 mm pocket means twice

The hardest question patients ask, Dr. Geisinger says, is "why now?" Someone who never missed a six-month cleaning is suddenly told they have 8 mm pockets. Those pockets didn't appear overnight. The honest answer is usually a mix of not diagnosing, not treating, or "good enough" care that never reached below the gumline: repeated above-the-gum cleanings on someone who needed real gum treatment. The lecture's name for this is P.E.R.I.O.D. disease: Partially Effective, Redundant Instrumentation, Overlooking Disease. Cleaning only above the gums in a periodontitis patient improves plaque scores but doesn't shrink pockets or regain attachment. It actually raises bleeding and the number of 4 mm+ pockets, and shifts the bacteria under the gum toward nastier, oxygen-hating species (notably P. gingivalis). Something is not always better than nothing.

It's also why a 3 mm pocket can mean two different things. After gum treatment, the gum reattaches with a long junctional epithelium, a thin skin-like seal, instead of the strong fiber attachment of healthy gums. That seal breaks down more easily when inflamed. So a treated patient with 3 mm everywhere still isn't a "prophy" patient the way someone who never had gum disease would be. They still need the periodontal maintenance code and schedule, because the tissue itself is built differently, even when the numbers look normal.

The inflammatory burden, and why it isn't "just" a mouth problem

The lecture makes this concrete with PISA (periodontal inflamed surface area): the total area of inflamed pocket lining. A healthy mouth averages about 34 mm², roughly a paper cut. Even mild-to-moderate (Stage 1-2) periodontitis averages about 2,309 mm², about the size of a wound from a spreading skin infection with early Ludwig's angina. That's why gum disease counts as an inflammation load on the whole body, not a local nuisance. It's linked to more than 50 body-wide conditions, and a few links have hard numbers: periodontitis raised the odds of dying after COVID-19 about nine-fold and of hospitalization about five-fold in one comparison; in a COPD trial, real below-the-gum treatment cut lung flare-ups about twice as much as above-the-gum cleaning or nothing; and in a diabetes trial, intensive gum treatment (full-mouth deep cleaning, surgery where needed, 3-month maintenance) brought HbA1c down from 8.1% to 7.8% over a year, while the above-the-gum-only group went from 8.1% up to 8.3% and had three deaths recorded as adverse events.

Measuring risk with a tool instead of a gut feeling

Scoring tools estimate risk better than gut feeling. UniFe (Trombelli) scores five things from 0 to 4: cigarettes per day, diabetes control (HbA1c), number of pockets 5 mm or deeper, percent of sites that bleed, and bone loss divided by age. The total puts the patient in one of five risk levels. The Periodontal Risk Assessment (PRA) (Lang and Tonetti) and PreViser/PAT (Page) work the same way, combining exam, X-ray and lifestyle inputs into one risk level; UniFe and PreViser agreed fairly well when tested on the same patients. Newer AI tools (Pearl AI and Overjet were named) are joining them. None of them escape "garbage in, garbage out": they're only as good as the exam data you feed them.

Turning a risk tier into an actual recall plan

Once a patient is low, moderate or high risk, that level should change what you actually do:

  • Low risk: full gum exam every 6-12 months, X-rays every 12-24 months, professional cleaning every 6 months, normal home care (brush twice a day, clean between teeth once a day), diet advice, and tobacco prevention.
  • Moderate risk: full exam every 6-12 months plus a quick gum screen every 6 months, X-rays every 6-12 months, keep an eye on general health, cleaning plus spot deep-cleaning every 4-6 months, fix plaque traps, think about a local antimicrobial, surgery if needed to stop disease or repair defects, help quitting tobacco, extra hygiene tools (water or air flosser, rinses, probiotics), and check how well they keep up.
  • High risk: full exam every 6-12 months plus a screen every 3 months, X-rays every 6 months, close health monitoring with physician consults, cleaning plus deep-cleaning every 2-4 months, think about systemic or local antibiotics, surgery likely, and the same home-care and quit-tobacco package, checked more closely.
Why maintenance intervals are what they are

Treated patients who skip maintenance lose teeth about twice as often as those who come back, and more frequent visits go with fewer teeth lost. Yet only about 30-40% of patients stick with maintenance. The 3-month interval isn't random: harmful bacteria start moving back under the gum 4-8 weeks after treatment, and by 9-11 weeks they can be back near where they started. A 3-month recall lands inside that window. Patients in active braces are seen even more often (about every 4-6 weeks), partly because that's when the braces get adjusted, and partly because inflammation while teeth are moving can throw off the balance of bone building and bone removal, risking real bone loss if plaque isn't tightly controlled. Coming regularly matters, not just the total number of visits, and it matters most for Stage 3-4 and Grade C patients: one who skips more than a year of maintenance over five years has about 2.5 times the odds of losing a tooth to gum disease.

Communicating risk so patients actually act on it

The number one reason patients say no to a gum treatment plan is that they don't trust their dental provider. The most trusted person in the office by far is the hygienist, not the dentist, which is why the whole team needs to give the same message. 62% of patients delay, switch dentists, get a second opinion, or refuse because they disagree with or doubt the diagnosis. Cost is rarely the real reason: patients say they'd pay about $633.63 per tooth to keep it. Cost becomes the objection when they feel rushed, can't ask questions, sense the team disagreeing, or aren't offered ways to manage the cost. In other words, when they don't yet feel you care about them.

A stage-and-grade diagnosis ("Stage 2 Grade B periodontitis") gives everyone the same precise words. The lecture models moving a patient from cleanings to real treatment as a short conversation: say what you've been tracking and what it shows (the problem); explain plainly that once pockets are deeper than home care can reach, about 1.5-2 mm, bacteria settle in under the gum (the consequence); and lay out the "prescribed" (not just "proposed") plan and what it gains compared with doing nothing (the solution). The best predictors of a good long-term result are the same list this whole session covers: home hygiene, keeping up with maintenance, bleeding, pockets left after treatment, bite, bone loss for age, body-wide and genetic factors, and smoking.

In class: the three prognosis systems, compared

A prognosis is a prediction of how a tooth (or mouth) will do. The in-class Slido review, which Dr. Geisinger hinted "might inform the midterm," was about telling the three systems apart by what each one is asking, not by memorizing lists. McGuire & Nunn asks: can we keep this tooth? Most of the class guessed "will the disease get worse," which is wrong. Its order is good, fair, poor, questionable, hopeless, and the classic mistake is swapping poor and questionable. A "poor" tooth (lost attachment, Class II furcation, some looseness) can be kept, just with a lot of effort. A "questionable" tooth is one we honestly aren't sure we can keep, and it won't stay in that category: it either gets worse and becomes hopeless, or improves and moves up to poor.

How accurate is it? Every statement in the poll was true. It's right about 80% of the time overall (81% at 8 years). Take out the teeth rated "good" and it drops to about 50%, a coin flip. On average teeth do better than predicted, and even "hopeless" teeth in well-maintained patients often last much longer than expected. The exceptions are smokers and people with very poor hygiene, and even very poor hygiene matches the prediction if those patients keep coming to maintenance. Most teeth leave the mouth because a dentist pulls them, not because they fall out on their own (unlike implants, which often do).

McGuire & Nunn can be given for one tooth or the whole mouth, and as a diagnostic prognosis (what happens if the patient gets no treatment) or a therapeutic prognosis (how the recommended treatment changes things). The therapeutic version is a great way to show patients what treatment buys them. Kwok & Caton asks: can we stop the disease (get periodontal stability) with treatment? Answers run likely, don't know, unlikely. That's why "questionable" sits in the middle of its scale, and why it can only be therapeutic. It's the better pick for a medically complex patient, because quitting smoking or vaping and getting an A1c under control become part of the treatment it's judging. Miller & McEntire was studied only on molars. It uses numbers (A1c, smoking and other factors each get a score), and since it was built from patients who got 30 years of treatment and maintenance, it's therapeutic too. Smoking is its biggest single factor: about 296% more likely to lose those molars. The one-line summary: only McGuire & Nunn can be diagnostic; all three can be therapeutic.

In class: three cases, all Stage 3

A 78-year-old (generally healthy with mild issues, on a statin and baby aspirin, #17 lost to a root-canal perforation) had mostly horizontal bone loss of about 30%, 5 mm or more of attachment loss between teeth at her worst site, and a Class II furcation. That's generalized Stage 3, Grade B, and her missing teeth were lost to cavities, not gum disease. First check the chart is right: was recession on the tongue side recorded? Her Kwok & Caton prognosis was questionable, because flat bone loss and furcations are hard to regrow. Plan: maintenance every 3 months (bacteria refill in about 9-11 weeks, and once someone has had periodontitis they stay higher-risk even when healthy), adjust her bite for trauma from chewing forces, and watch the recession. The PRA spider-web chart (bleeding, 5 mm+ sites, missing teeth, % bone loss, smoking) said to keep doing what she's doing.

A 13-year-old with little plaque or inflammation had 8-11 mm pockets on her first molars and #14 in a molar-incisor pattern: localized Stage 3, Grade C. Deep, narrow vertical defects respond well to regrowing bone (bone graft, membrane, maybe a growth-factor product), filling about 70-75%, and young people heal better. So with treatment her McGuire & Nunn prognosis is good to fair overall, the affected teeth fair; without treatment it would be poor to questionable. Regrowing bone in the defect that set the stage is the only way to move someone back down from Stage 3. About 70% of kids with this around-puberty pattern have neutrophils (first-responder white blood cells) that don't move toward infection properly, which is why the first teeth to come in are hit hardest. About 70% of those whose disease later spreads use nicotine. She needs lifelong, more frequent maintenance and a strong anti-nicotine talk.

A 75-year-old former smoker with bleeding at about 80% of sites, 7-9 mm pockets, and both vertical and flat bone loss is Stage 3, Grade C. Her overall McGuire & Nunn prognosis with no treatment is poor, even though individual teeth range from good to hopeless, which is why per-tooth prognoses are useful. With good cooperation plus bone reshaping or regrowing surgery, it improves to fair. If she later gets diabetes (A1c 8.8%), her grade can't go past C, but her PRA risk chart balloons. That's the point of keeping prognosis and risk tools separate from stage and grade: they catch differences the diagnosis can't.

The closing numbers: about 10% of people resist periodontitis no matter their hygiene, 10-15% are at risk for severe disease, and 20-25% don't respond to standard treatment. Results depend on what patients control (hygiene, showing up for maintenance), exam findings (bleeding, leftover pockets, bite trauma, bone loss for age), and body-wide, genetic and nicotine factors.
plain.phase1-therapy:
Phase I is the non-surgical first step every gum patient gets, whatever their stage. These notes combine the 2026 slide deck with the recorded class. Dr. Kaur explained that D2 goes a step past D1. Instead of basics, it covers treatment: when it works, when it doesn't, and what the options are, so you're ready for clinic next year. She spent class on the exam and the reasons behind treatment, and saved the instrument details for the upcoming PCD (hands-on) sessions.

What's on the midterm (Dr. Kaur's email after class): instruments, ultrasonic scalers and polishing won't be tested. Study the class discussion and the slides up to failure of therapy. In these notes, that's everything down to the section on the re-evaluation and when treatment "fails." The sections after it are marked.
Flagged in class: about the diagram showing how bacteria and the body's immune response move a patient from health to gingivitis to periodontitis, she said "has anybody been counting? That's going to be on the quiz." Know what starts the disease, what makes it worse, and which one a deep cleaning actually treats.
Start from the diagnosis

Every patient fits one of three big groups: healthy gums, gingivitis (gum inflammation only) or periodontitis (gum disease that has destroyed bone). Healthy gums and gingivitis can each happen on a full-height set of supporting tissues (intact periodontium) or on one that has already lost some height (reduced periodontium). Periodontitis can't happen on an intact periodontium, because bone loss is what makes it periodontitis. You can't tell the three apart just by looking at a photo or into the mouth. You need the full gum chart (pocket depths, recession, attachment loss, furcations, loose teeth, how the gums look) plus the X-rays.

The exam: plaque and gum health

A full gum exam checks home hygiene (plaque score), gum health, pocket depths, attachment, furcations, the gum-to-cheek-lining border, loose teeth, the bite, and X-rays. It always starts with plaque, because plaque is the main cause of gum disease. There are two ways to record it. You can slide the probe about 1 mm into the gum crevice (this isn't measuring the pocket) and score each spot 1 if plaque comes out on the probe and 0 if not. Or the patient chews a disclosing tablet (lavender or pink in the clinic), rinses briefly, and you wipe the extra dye off the cheeks and tongue, show them in a mirror and record the score. Both methods only record whether plaque is there or not, not how much. Measuring amount (near the gum only, half the tooth, the whole tooth) at every spot would take far too long.

Gum health is judged by color (redness), texture (swelling), bleeding when probed (BOP) and a gingival index. Bleeding is recorded while you probe: 1 if the spot bleeds, 0 if not. Late bleeding counts. After you've moved on a couple of teeth or to the next quarter of the mouth, look back. Any earlier spot that has started bleeding still gets a 1.

Not every periodontitis patient looks the same, because other factors change how the gums appear. Smoking hides inflammation: nicotine squeezes blood vessels, so the gums often look bluish-gray instead of puffy and bleeding. Diabetes makes inflammation look worse. Gum overgrowth caused by a medication tells you something in the medical history is adding to the picture. The class example was a patient with high blood pressure taking amlodipine (a calcium channel blocker). The gums were bulging, mostly between the teeth, and more on the cheek/lip side than the tongue/palate side. The four patients shown, all from the student clinic, all had periodontitis. Their gums looked quite different, including one with uncontrolled diabetes who was also on a calcium channel blocker.

Probing, recession and CAL

Probing records six spots per tooth (DB, B, MB, DL, L, ML), taking the deepest reading at each. Probing depth runs from the gum edge to the bottom of the pocket. Recession runs from the CEJ (the line where enamel meets root) to the gum edge. Clinical attachment level runs from the CEJ to the bottom of the pocket, so CAL = probing depth + recession. The deck's pair: a 7 mm pocket with no recession and a 2 mm pocket with 5 mm of recession both have a CAL of 7 mm.

Her big point: in healthy gums, pocket depth is not the same as attachment level. Healthy gum sits a little above the CEJ and covers it. Recession is positive when the gum has pulled back and you can see the CEJ. It's negative when the gum edge sits above the CEJ: −1, −2, −3, or even more with medication-caused overgrowth. Add it with its sign. A 5 mm pocket with −3 mm recession is a CAL of 2 mm. Skip the recession and the same spot reads 5 mm, which would point to Stage 3 or 4 disease even if the X-rays show only about 20% bone loss. Pocket depths, attachment levels and X-rays should all tell the same story.

The same mistake happens in Salud, the charting software. If you leave recession blank, or type 0 without checking whether it's really positive or negative, Salud makes CAL equal to pocket depth. A blank over-diagnoses disease, and an automatic zero is inaccurate too. Enter the real number with its sign and Salud does the math correctly.

To measure negative recession you have to feel the CEJ, since you can't see it. Slide the probe to the bottom of the pocket, then slowly pull it out until you feel the rough CEJ. The millimeters still under the gum at that point are the negative recession, which you subtract from the pocket depth. It's harder with lots of inflammation or overgrowth (both caused by disease), with altered passive eruption (a normal variation), and with tartar or filling edges that can feel like a CEJ. On eruption: as a tooth comes in, active eruption is the tooth moving up to meet the opposite tooth, and passive eruption is the gum moving down to settle at the CEJ. In altered passive eruption the gum never moves down, so its edge stays well above the CEJ. Getting good at this takes practice.

The probe is the most important exam tool. Press lightly, feel for the springy stop, and keep it parallel to the tooth. Between teeth, don't stop at the corner of the tooth (the line angle). Go past it and under the contact point (front teeth) or contact area (back teeth), tilting slightly toward the spot just below the contact.

When you can't probe yet: debridement

Debridement isn't a treatment. You never do it to treat disease, and it should never be combined with scaling and root planing (deep cleaning). The only reason to do it is tartar so heavy that you can't see or feel the gum edge, so you can't take any measurements. There's only a full-mouth debridement code, no half-mouth or single-area version. It's meant for tartar so widespread it covers even the chewing surfaces, which is rare. Insurance won't pay for debridement and a gum exam at the same visit: if you couldn't measure before, the gums won't be ready right after. So in private practice the patient usually comes back in about two weeks for the full chart.

School is more flexible. The first gum charting is free, so after clearing a patch of heavy tartar you can do the full chart at the same visit if the gums look okay. Check with your faculty, who may want to let the gums settle for two weeks. Combining saves the patient a trip. In private practice you can also choose not to charge for a small debridement, though a packed hygiene schedule is often a reason to split visits anyway.

Furcations: named classes, not millimeters

A furcation is where a tooth's roots split. It's checked with the Nabers probe, which is curved with light and dark bands every 3 mm, alongside X-rays. Even so, the grading used here is the Glickman classification, which is based on what you feel, not a millimeter count. Class I does not mean "3 mm or less."

  • Class I, just starting. The probe barely catches. Usually no treatment. Easy to keep stable as long as the attachment and pocket don't get worse.
  • Class II, a dead end. The probe goes clearly into the furcation, but bone still stands on the far side (probe from the cheek side and the palate/tongue-side bone is still there). Because it's a contained pocket with depth, it's the class best suited to regrowing bone (regeneration).
  • Class III, all the way through. The hardest to treat. Nothing contains it, so it can't regrow.
  • Class IV. A Class III where the gum has also pulled back (naturally or by surgery), so you can see through it. The patient can clean it with little brushes or a water flosser, but the exposed roots risk sensitivity and root cavities. A cavity in a furcation makes the tooth hopeless (it will need to come out), so watch these teeth closely at every maintenance visit.

Her cases: an upper molar (#3) with furcation involvement was the only back support for a bridge. Instead of pulling it, they turned the Class III into a Class IV (cleaned it and moved the gum down so the patient could reach it). That patient is still doing well. Another patient given the same treatment got a large cavity under the roof of the furcation.

Gum border, loose teeth and the bite

The gum border check asks how much firm (keratinized) gum the patient has. Measure its width directly, or use the rolling technique: roll the loose cheek lining up toward the teeth until it stops at the mucogingival junction (where firm gum begins). This matters around implants as well as teeth.

Looseness is checked with two rigid, blunt instrument handles, one on each side of the tooth, and graded on the Miller scale: 0 is normal, 1 is a little more than normal (under 1 mm), 2 is moderately more (between 1 and 2 mm), and 3 is severe side-to-side movement plus the tooth can be pushed down into its socket. A tooth that pushes down into its socket is ready to come out. That's looseness at rest. Fremitus is looseness while the teeth work. Put a finger on the root while the patient taps their teeth together and feel for vibration. It can go up-and-down and/or side-to-side, and you usually feel it rather than see it. If you feel fremitus, find out why that tooth is taking so much force. In the class example, missing back teeth meant the premolars were doing the molars' job.

The gum chart has no box for bite findings, so put them in the notes section: wear patterns, acid erosion, vertical bone defects and whether they link to a bite problem, and grinding or clenching. This matters because a loose tooth isn't always just gum disease. It can be too much biting force on a tooth that has already lost support, from missing back teeth, grinding, or overjet and overbite. Treating a 5 mm pocket won't fix grade 2 looseness unless the bite is fixed too. The deck's list of bite warning signs: grinding or clenching habits, loose teeth, fremitus, drifting teeth, open contacts, unusual wear and wear facets, possible jaw-joint pain, vertical bone defects and a widened ligament space on X-ray.

X-rays, before you touch the patient

Before you take any measurements, X-rays show whether there's bone loss, whether it's in a few spots or all over, and its pattern (flat, vertical, or both). They also show tipped teeth, fused roots, roots too close together (important for surgery and deep cleaning), tartar, how close the sinus is, and an infection at a root tip (#7 in the class X-ray). Seeing tartar on an X-ray should make you "a little bit of both" sad and excited. Sad the patient got to that point, excited because now you know the cause and it's something you can remove. Once tartar has formed the patient can't brush it off, so your job matters even more.

Her tip: when you start a deep cleaning (or even a regular cleaning), don't open the chart to hunt for deep pockets. Your instrument will find the pocket, and the bottom of the pocket is where you stop. Open the X-rays instead (take screenshots, since Salud logs you out). Then roughness on #14-15 matches tartar you already saw, and pus or a draining spot on #7 matches the root-tip infection. Look at the X-rays before you start measuring.

Why Phase I works: bacteria start it, the body drives it

Plaque bacteria start the disease. The body's immune response is what makes it get worse. In health the immune system handles the bacteria quickly and the bacteria aren't very harmful, so disease never shows. In gingivitis the bacteria change and the attack gets stronger. The body still wins, but it takes longer: more immune cells (T cells and B cells) join the first responders (neutrophils), and you see inflammation for days to a couple of weeks. Not everyone moves from reversible inflammation to permanent damage. Those who do have an immune system that overreacts and releases inflammatory signals (cytokines). Environment, genes, habits and gene-switching (epigenetic) factors add to the risk. The result is lost attachment, lost bone, and damage to the ligament, root surface and bone around the tooth.

Deep cleaning targets the bacteria, yet bacteria cause only about 25% of the damage. About 75% comes from the body's own inflammatory signals and bone-dissolving cells (osteoclasts). Bacteria bring toxins (endotoxin, also called lipopolysaccharide), not osteoclasts. Removing the bacteria calms the body's response. Some patients still have disease after good home care and the best cleaning or surgery. For them, drugs can calm the body's response directly. That's host modulation, or "periodontal medicine," which Dr. Litz covers later. Bacteria coat tartar and live inside its tiny channels, and tartar and plaque also act as irritants the body reacts to.

The goals of removing them: less inflammation, a shift in the pocket bacteria from the harmful gram-negative kind toward gram-positive (healthy mouths still have bacteria, just friendlier ones), and stopping the disease from getting worse. Deep cleaning doesn't undo the damage. Lost bone and attachment stay lost, which is why periodontitis is called irreversible. And getting rid of pockets is not the reason for deep cleaning, even though pockets do shrink. A pocket is a space the patient can't clean, full of more harmful bacteria. Phase I changes that environment.

How pockets shrink, and why you check at 4-6 weeks

Two things make a pocket shallower. At the top: inflamed gum is swollen with extra cells and fluid. As it calms down the gum shrinks, which you measure as more recession. At the bottom: disease had broken both the thin seal of gum cells against the tooth (the junctional epithelium, which is why the probe sank deeper) and the fibers holding the gum to the root. After cleaning, both reattach to the clean root. You measure in two dimensions, but the disease is three-dimensional.

The healing timeline: the gum seal (junctional epithelium) takes 7-10 days, the fiber reattachment takes 4-6 weeks, and the fibers mature and line up over 3-6 months. That's why the patient comes back at 4-6 weeks. You see the full result by then, and research shows waiting longer doesn't shrink the pocket any further. The deck says it a bit differently: pockets shrink most in the first 4 weeks, the seal between gum and tooth re-forms in 2-4 weeks, and healing can keep going for 9-12 months. Know both. The deck's "a 6 mm pocket might become 5 or 4.5" numbers are just for a sense of scale. She said you don't need to memorize them.

The words (and the billing codes)

Scaling removes soft and hard buildup from teeth, roots and any bridges or dentures, both above and below the gum. If you're asked whether scaling is above or below the gum, the answer is both. Root planing stays below the gum and only works on roots. It smooths away rough, tartar-packed or contaminated root surface until there are no ridges, rough spots or catches. In practice you do both together.

A prophylaxis ("prophy") is a preventive cleaning, not a treatment, for someone who has never had periodontitis (healthy gums or gingivitis). Tartar a little below the gum doesn't mean periodontitis: everyone has a shallow crevice, and tartar 1-2 mm down is removed as part of the prophy. Periodontal maintenance is ongoing support for someone already treated for periodontitis, to keep the disease from coming back, with their home care checked every visit. The two terms don't mean the same thing. A maintenance patient with mostly 1-3 mm pockets, a few leftover 4s and one 5 can stay on maintenance if their hygiene is good, those spots don't bleed, the gums look healthy and the X-rays show no new bone loss. Deep cleaning just the few leftover deep pockets is officially part of maintenance.

Scaling in the presence of gingival inflammation (D4346) sits between a prophy and a deep cleaning. It's for someone never diagnosed with periodontitis, with no bone loss, but with heavy, widespread gum inflammation caused by plaque and tartar, so a simple prophy doesn't cover the work. At school it's done with perio faculty or a resident and gets a Phase I re-evaluation. The class case was a young patient (20s to early 30s) with a bridge of tartar on the tongue side of the teeth. What looked like bone loss around the premolars and front of the molars came from premolars pulled for braces and the tipping that followed, not from periodontitis. Diagnosis: widespread gum inflammation on a reduced periodontium in a patient without periodontitis (the deck calls it gingivitis on a reduced periodontium), treated with D4346. That patient had debridement, charting and treatment all in one visit. Full-mouth debridement (D4355) is a rough clean-out so the proper exam can happen at a later visit.

What the evidence says about how to do it

Splitting the deep cleaning into several visits doesn't really help: tartar left behind after several visits stays for the same reasons it stays after one (Anderson 1996). Hand instruments and ultrasonic (powered) scalers work about the same for shrinking pockets and regaining attachment, and adding under-the-gum rinsing with chlorhexidine, saline or peroxide adds nothing. In pockets 5 mm or deeper, the root isn't fully cleaned about 65% of the time (Greenstein 2000).

What makes it hard, as she taught it: deeper pockets are harder to reach, though a 5 mm pocket doesn't mean tartar gets left every time. Deep cleaning is done blind: you work by feel. Some bacteria swim into the gum lining, while cleaning only reaches the pocket (and it doesn't reliably wipe out A. actinomycetemcomitans). Fillings and crowns with overhanging, below-the-gum, open or rough edges collect plaque and are hard to clean around. Furcations and the natural grooves and dips in roots block access. Trying hard for a smooth root can take off too much root surface (cementum) and make teeth sensitive. And results depend on the patient's home care and the clinician's skill, which improves with practice.

The re-evaluation, and when it "fails"

Check back at 4-6 weeks: plaque scores, signs of inflammation, bleeding, pocket depths, recession, attachment, looseness, furcations and pus. This is where the decision about surgery is made. If there's still inflammation and the numbers haven't improved, check whether leftover tartar is the reason. You'll often feel it with the probe while re-measuring. If so, remove it (no charge) and re-check in two weeks. If you already got all the tartar the first time, more rounds of deep cleaning won't help. What helps is better home care.

"Failure of therapy" is a harsh phrase, because so much is out of your control. The body's response affects healing as well as disease. A smoker or someone with uncontrolled diabetes may not get the same short- or long-term result from your best cleaning. The deck's approach when Phase I doesn't work: look at how the gums responded, what tartar is left, the health history and risk factors, and maybe a plaque culture. Then choose antibiotics or antimicrobials, host-modulation drugs, a repeat cleaning, another re-evaluation, or Phase II, which is surgery to get rid of pockets.

The instruments (not on the midterm)

Dr. Kaur's email says instruments, ultrasonic scalers and polishing won't be on the midterm. In the slides they come after failure of therapy. The email is only about the midterm, so this can still show up on the final and in the hands-on instrument check.

She kept instruments light on purpose. They get covered in detail in the upcoming PCD sessions, and you don't need the numbers yet, though you will later. For now, your daily kit has three groups. The exam tools are the mirror, the gum probe, the Nabers probe for furcations, and a gum explorer. This isn't the cavity explorer. You use it after cleaning to check that roots feel smooth with no catches. Then come scalers and curettes. Every instrument has a handle, a shank (the neck) and a blade.

Scalers are mostly for above the gum. They reach only a little way under it (the deck says 1-2 mm; in class she said about 2-3, noting sources vary). Their strokes are short, strong and fast. Curettes go deep into the pocket with longer, slightly lighter strokes that take more time, though stubborn tartar can still need real pressure. The key difference is the blade. A scaler cuts on both sides. A Gracey curette cuts on one side only, so below the gum the side facing the gum can't cut it. Almost every curette in your kit is a Gracey, marked SG, each shaped for one area and cutting on one side. The one SC instrument is the universal curette, which, like a scaler, cuts on both sides.

The clinic has piezoelectric ultrasonic (vibrating) scalers along with hand instruments. They work below the gum too, but they can't root plane, so they won't leave the root smooth. Use them together: ultrasonic to knock off the heavy tartar, then hand instruments, then the ultrasonic again so its water spray flushes out the pocket.

From the deck, for later: gum hand instruments are mirrors, explorers, probes, scaling and root-planing tools, and polishing tools. The mirror lets you see indirectly, bounces light in, and holds the cheek or tongue back. The ODU 11/12 explorer is run over every surface of every tooth to feel for rough root. Its neck is shaped like the Gracey 11/12. Slide it in with the lower neck parallel to the tooth until you feel the slight resistance of the gum attachment, then stroke up-and-down and side-to-side with the side of the tip. The UNC-15 probe is 15 mm long. The exam kit is probe, explorer, Nabers probe, mirror and cotton pliers.

A sickle scaler has a pointed tip, a triangle-shaped cross-section and two cutting edges, and shouldn't be used much on exposed root. Hook it under the ledge of tartar and pull with short, strong strokes using the lower third of the blade. The H6/7 (straight neck) is for front teeth and the cheek/tongue sides of molars. The S204SD9 (neck bent at a right angle) is for the spaces between back teeth. Both are held at about 80° to the root. A curette has a rounded tip and a half-moon cross-section and works above and below the gum. A universal curette (Columbia 13/14) has two cutting edges. An area-specific Gracey has one.

Gracey curettes have a 70° blade angle, one cutting edge (the lower one), and a rounded back so they don't cut the gum. The lower neck should sit parallel to the tooth. Slide it in nearly flat (closed), then open it to 70-80° against the root to work. Which one goes where: 3/4 (or 1/2, 7/8) for all surfaces of front teeth (the demo slide adds premolars) and deep tartar. 11/12 for the mesial (front-facing) surfaces of back teeth plus the cheek/tongue sides of molars. 15/16 as another mesial tool for back teeth. 13/14 for the distal (back-facing) surfaces of back teeth. The 13/14 has more bends in its neck than the 11/12 and is pulled from root toward crown or from back toward front.

Ultrasonic scalers come in two types. Magnetostrictive: electricity makes the nickel-iron metal stack in the insert change shape and vibrate in an oval-to-circular pattern, about 18,000-42,000 times a second, so every side of the tip can clean. Piezoelectric: electricity vibrates crystals in the handpiece, the tip moves back and forth in a line, and mainly its sides do the work. For implants, probes are marked in 3 mm bands (3-6-9-12 or 3-6-8-11), and the listed tools are front and back sickle scalers plus the Columbia 4R/4L.

Technique (not on the midterm)
Don't forget (the deck's own emphasis): modified pen grasp and a finger rest.

A finger rest (fulcrum) steadies your hand. There are four: conventional (on the teeth right next to where you're working), cross-arch (on the other side of the same jaw), opposite-arch (on the other jaw), and finger-on-finger (on the index finger or thumb of your other hand). How you fit the instrument to the tooth depends on the gum (tough and fibrous vs. puffy and bleeding), how bad the disease is (how easily the gum moves aside, the space between teeth), and how stuck-on the tartar is.

An exploratory stroke is light, with the tool fitted to the tooth, to map the pocket and find tartar. A working stroke uses a firm grip with pressure through the tip. Scaling strokes are short, overlapping, strong and controlled. Root-planing strokes are longer and lighter, like shaving. You check your work during the visit by feeling the root with an explorer, and at re-evaluation by how the gums respond: less redness, swelling and bleeding. The patient's home care weighs heavily on that result. The spots most often missed are the CEJ, furcation entrances, line angles (corners of the teeth), and hard-to-reach areas, especially the back surfaces of back teeth.

To polish or not to polish (not on the midterm)

For polishing: it removes stain that brushing and scaling leave behind, preps teeth for sealants, fluoride gels and varnishes, and patients like it. Against: 30 seconds with pumice can take off up to 4 µm of enamel, and that outer layer has the most fluoride. A coarse paste can leave the surface rougher than before. Steady pressure from a fast-spinning rubber cup can hurt and may heat the nerve. A rubber cup with pumice for 2 minutes can strip the thin lining inside the gum pocket completely, and pumice can get pushed under the gum. If you polish, use a low-abrasion paste on a slow handpiece with little heat, hold the cup at 90° to the tooth, and press lightly on and off. (Polishing comes from the deck. It wasn't covered in the recorded class.)
plain.resective-furcation:
Session 5 has two parts, both by Dr. Litz. Furcation Management is his recorded lecture, which the Oct 15 quiz covered. Resective Osseous Surgery he taught in person on Oct 15, after the quiz; that class also went back over the furcation points he cares about most.

Furcation vs. furcation defect

A furcation is the normal spot on a tooth with more than one root (premolars and molars) where the roots split apart. Every such tooth has one. A furcation defect is what gum disease does to it: the gum and bone between the roots get destroyed, and attachment is lost down into that space. The single most important point of the lecture, repeated again and again: once gum disease reaches the furcation, the tooth's outlook drops sharply. Furcations are very hard for us to clean and even harder for patients, so look for them at every exam, cleaning and maintenance visit.

Words to know, and the root trunk

The root trunk is the solid part of the root from the CEJ (where enamel meets root) down to where the roots first split. The separate roots below it are also called root cones. The root complex is the whole root, trunk plus cones. The fornix is the roof of the furcation, and divergence is how far apart the roots spread, in millimeters.

About 30% of a molar's attachment is on the root trunk and 70% on the separate roots. A short root trunk is a risk: if the trunk is only 2 mm long, 2 mm of attachment loss already opens the furcation. A long root trunk protects at first, because it takes much more loss to reach the furcation. But once the furcation is reached, a long trunk is bad news: these teeth usually can't have a root removed, and since a long trunk means short roots, there's little support left by then.

Where the furcation openings are

He called these numbers very important (from a 1979 study by Bower), measured down from the CEJ. On the upper first molar, which has three openings: the front (mesial) one about 3.6 mm down, the cheek-side (buccal) one about 4.2 mm, and the back (distal) one about 4.8 mm. Another slide rounds these to about 3.5, 4 and 5 mm. On the lower first molar, which has two: cheek side about 2.4 mm and tongue side about 2.5 mm. Those are much shallower, so a 4-5 mm pocket on a lower molar may already mean an open furcation. (The class exam-review guide gives the upper numbers as 3, 3.5 and 5 mm; same order.)

On upper molars, the cheek-side opening is usually the narrowest, because the two cheek-side roots sit close together. The first molar's root trunk is usually shorter than the second molar's. Lower molars tilt toward the tongue, which puts the tongue-side opening a little deeper than the cheek side (a slide also gives it as more than 4 mm down and more than 0.75 mm wide). The lower molar's front root is wide cheek-to-tongue and pinched in the middle like an hourglass or kidney bean, with grooves facing the furcation.
