Upper premolars have two roots about 40% of the time, with the split about 8 mm down: a long trunk with short roots. The upper first premolar always has a groove on its front (mesial) surface (about 0.5 mm deep) next to the furcation, which floss slides right past even when used well.

Why furcations are so hard to clean

81% of furcation openings are under 1 mm wide and 58% are under 0.75 mm, but a curette blade is 0.75-1.10 mm wide. So most of the time the blade simply doesn't fit, no matter how good the numbing, the time or the instrument; even thin ultrasonic tips struggle. His extracted molar showed it: the rounded outer root was smooth as glass, while inside the furcation, after several deep cleanings, tartar and inflamed tissue remained. Rounded (convex) surfaces are easy to clean; hollowed (concave) ones are much harder.

The root surfaces facing into the furcation usually have dips. On the upper first molar, the front cheek-side root has a 0.3 mm dip 94% of the time, the back cheek-side root a 0.1 mm dip 31% of the time, and the palate root a 0.1 mm dip 17% of the time. The lower first molar is worse: the front root has a 0.7 mm dip every time, and the back root a 0.5 mm dip 99% of the time. During a deep cleaning you can't see these, and patients have almost no chance of cleaning them daily.

Which furcations are affected most

Teeth with short root trunks get furcation problems after only a little attachment loss, and usually do worse than single-rooted teeth. Upper molars are affected more often than lower molars. On upper molars, the cheek-side furcation is affected most, then the front one, then the back one. On lower molars, the cheek-side furcation is affected most.

What causes it, and what makes it worse

The main cause is ongoing attachment loss from gum disease, which comes from plaque. He expects that question on every perio exam and on boards. Other things add to it:

  • How long the root trunk is, which affects both whether the furcation gets involved and which treatments are possible.
  • Root shape: curved or fluted roots are easier to puncture during a root canal, which can cause furcation problems.
  • How far apart the roots are: roots that sit close together or are fused keep instruments out; widely spread roots are easier to treat.
  • Cervical enamel projections (CEPs): below.
  • Enamel pearls: little balls of enamel, most often in molar furcations. Gum tissue can't attach to enamel, and the bump holds plaque. On an x-ray, a white half-circle in the furcation suggests one. Small ones can be ground off, usually after opening the gum.
  • Dental work: a filling or crown edge that overhangs near a furcation traps plaque and leads to bone and attachment loss. Edges below the gumline should stay inside the gum pocket.
  • Intermediate bifurcation ridge: a rounded ridge of root surface running front-to-back across the furcation opening of a lower molar, joining the two roots. It leaves a domed hollow above it that traps plaque where no one can reach once it's exposed.
Cervical enamel projections

He called these a definite test question, and something to know for life. A CEP is a thin, pointed strip of enamel reaching down from the CEJ toward or into the furcation, like a widow's peak. It happens when enamel formation doesn't stop before the root starts forming. Because gum tissue can't attach to enamel, the gum just lies on top of it, and the CEP acts like a funnel steering plaque straight into the furcation. CEPs show up on about 30% of lower molars and 15% of upper molars, more often on second molars and on the cheek side.

They're graded by how far down they reach:

  • Grade 1: the CEJ clearly dips down toward the furcation.
  • Grade 2: the enamel gets close to the furcation but doesn't enter it.
  • Grade 3: the enamel reaches into the furcation.

The key fact for treatment: new attachment won't form on enamel. If there's no bone or attachment loss, often the case with Grades 1 and 2, usually leave it and watch it. If there is loss, remove the CEP. Thin enamel comes off with a diamond or finishing bur (usually after opening the gum, sometimes without if it's very shallow). Thicker enamel can be removed carefully without reaching the nerve, and on a living tooth, warn the patient it may be sensitive to hot and cold. His bigger rule: if one furcation is involved in a mouth that's otherwise healthy, look for a CEP. One deep spot on one tooth means something about that tooth is different: a CEP, an overhang, leftover cement, or a cracked root under a root canal.

Grading furcations

Furcations are checked with the curved Nabers probe, slid gently under the gum to feel for the opening; it takes seconds. The Glickman grades (1953), the system he uses:

  • Grade I: early. You can feel the opening, but the bone between the roots is intact and the probe can't hook in.
  • Grade II: some bone between the roots is gone, but not all the way through. The probe hooks in and catches when pulled up.
  • Grade III: all the way through; the probe goes in one side and out the other.
  • Grade IV: all the way through, and the gum has pulled back so you can see through it.

The Hamp system (1975), common among periodontists, uses millimeters of sideways loss: degree 1, under 3 mm in; degree 2, more than 3 mm but not through; degree 3, all the way through. Both Glickman and Hamp measure sideways (horizontal) loss. Tarnow and Fletcher (1984) add the up-and-down (vertical) depth in steps of 3 mm: A, 0-3 mm; B, 4-6 mm; C, 7 mm or more. Deeper means a worse outlook.

Finding them: probing and x-rays

The cheek-side opening of upper molars and both openings of lower molars are easy to reach. On upper molars, the front (mesiopalatal) opening sits toward the palate, so probe it from the palate side. The back (distopalatal) opening sits about halfway across, so it can be probed from either side.

On x-rays, bone loss in a furcation can come from gum disease, a root canal infection, a punctured root or bite trauma. Lower molars, with two roots, show it clearly. Upper molars are harder because roots overlap on the film: bone loss at the cheek-side furcation is often hidden behind the palate root. Loss at the front or back openings often shows as a furcation arrow, a small dark triangle pointing into the furcation. About 30-55% of Grade II or III furcations show one. If you see an arrow, a furcation problem is very likely, but many don't show one, so an arrow must never be the only test.

His rule for all of dentistry: examine the patient first, reach a diagnosis, then use x-rays to confirm it. Take both periapical x-rays and vertical bitewings. In one study (Ross and Thompson, 1980), the clinical exam alone found furcation problems in only 3% of upper and 9% of lower molars; adding x-rays raised that to 65% of upper but only 23% of lower molars. Use both.

Deciding whether to treat

Just having a furcation involved doesn't automatically mean it needs treatment. Active gum disease and anything nearby that's making it worse decide that. Removing plaque and tartar is always the most important step, but the cause also has to go: leave a CEP, an overhang or leftover tartar, and the loss continues. Early furcation problems usually need no treatment unless there's a local cause you can fix. Moderate to advanced ones have a lot of sideways loss; the aim is an area the patient and hygienist can keep clean, and the best long-term approach is to shrink or get rid of the furcation.

Treatment has two goals: 1. get the plaque off the exposed root surfaces, and 2. leave a shape the patient can clean. Without surgery: deep cleaning (Phase I), antibiotics placed in the pocket after cleaning (a later lecture), and reshaping the tooth at the furcation opening (furcation plasty). With surgery: opening the gum to clean, making a tunnel, regrowing bone (regeneration), removing a root, or pulling the tooth and placing an implant.

By class: Class I, deep cleaning, fixing local causes and smoothing the opening. Class II, smoothing the opening, regrowing bone (GTR), removing a root, or extraction. Class III, a tunnel, removing a root, or extraction. Whether a tooth is worth treating also depends on how bad the furcation is (Class I and shallow Class II do better), how much support is left around the whole tooth, pocket depths, looseness, root canal problems, the bite, how useful the tooth is (a lower molar with nothing biting against it may not be worth saving), the patient's health, and their brushing and flossing. Nothing works if the patient can't keep it clean.

Surgical options

The simplest is opening a gum flap to clean: cuts around the teeth and lifting the gum and its lining give a view in. If the bone loss is sideways only, not straight down, a thorough cleaning often calms the inflammation and shrinks the pocket. Reshaping the tooth (odontoplasty: removing a CEP, smoothing a ridge) or the bone (osteoplasty) makes the furcation shallower and easier to clean.

Regrowing bone needs the right patient and tooth. Poor candidates: uncontrolled diabetes, a weak immune system, smoking, or poor home care. The best teeth are lower molars and the cheek-side furcation of upper molars, at degree II. The front and back furcations of upper molars are much harder because they're hard to reach. At degree III, regrowing bone does no better than ordinary surgery. Things in its favor: thicker gums, no gum recession, and higher bone between the teeth. Roots sitting very close can get in the way; a previous root canal does not rule it out. The steps: open the gum, clean the root thoroughly (without this nothing grows back), remove any enamel projections or pearls, pack in bone graft and/or cover it with a membrane held by a dissolving sling stitch, close the gum over it, and no brushing or flossing there for up to 4 weeks (chlorhexidine rinse instead). About a year later, an x-ray shows whether bone filled in.

Tunneling purposely removes bone to open the furcation all the way through, creating a Glickman Grade IV on purpose, so the patient can push a small brush through. It's for deep Class II and Class III, and only on lower molars with long, well-spread roots. The catch: cavities in tunneled molars are common, since root surfaces decay fast. It's rarely done now that implants exist.

Root resection (root amputation) cuts off one or more roots where they meet the furcation, keeping the crown and the other roots. The root removed most often is the back cheek-side (distobuccal) root of the upper first molar. It's for deep Class II and Class III, gets rid of the furcation, and means the patient also needs a root canal and new dental work. It's still used, for example when a lower molar holding up a bridge (already root-canal treated) cracks one root while the other is sound: remove the cracked root and keep the bridge. Hemisection removes a root plus the part of the crown above it, usually on lower molars, making a two-rooted tooth into a one-rooted one. Implants have made it much rarer: it takes a root canal specialist, then the periodontist, then the restorative dentist, over many costly visits.

The order for removing a root: the root canal first, with the opening filled directly with amalgam or composite; a temporary crown; then separating and removing the root, without exposing the bone between the roots, leaving bits of the furcation roof, punching into the canals, or leaving sharp corners; then gum surgery to remove bone defects around the remaining roots, keeping the temporary crown's edges at least 3 mm above the bone; and finally the permanent crown or bridge, on a rigid framework and with a bite that keeps sideways forces low.

In class: the furcation points he repeated

Before the new topic, Dr. Litz went back over the recorded lecture. Every molar has a furcation; the trouble is a furcation defect, and once gum disease reaches the furcation the tooth's outlook drops sharply, because we can barely clean it and the patient almost never can. He asked again for the opening depths ("I want you to know these numbers"): upper first molar front-palate side 3.6, cheek side 4.2, back-palate side 4.8 mm; lower molar cheek side 2.4 and tongue side 2.5 mm. So when a molar probes 4, 5 or 6 mm, assume a furcation is already open. Most openings are narrower than a curette blade, and the root walls inside the furcation are dented inward, which hides tartar. Upper molars break down partly because their bone is less dense and the cheek-side bone is thin. A thin enamel projection usually comes off with a finishing bur in light strokes; warn the patient about cold sensitivity if it's thick. One deep spot in an otherwise healthy mouth means something is wrong with that one tooth: an enamel projection, an overhanging filling, leftover cement, or a cracked root on a root-canal-treated molar, which means the tooth comes out. He checks every molar with a curved Nabers probe and uses the Glickman grades, as the school does.

Phase I, the recheck, and when surgery comes in

In gum care, Phase I is home-care teaching (always first), a deep cleaning, fixing things that trap plaque (overhanging fillings, open contacts, reshaping enamel projections, which often can only be reached in surgery), and the recheck. Phase II is surgery, followed by regular maintenance visits. Phase I calms the inflammation, shrinks pockets that were only deep because the gum was swollen, firms up the tissue so it bleeds less and holds together in surgery, and above all aims for a mouth the patient can keep clean. He repeats that goal constantly: we clean their teeth a few times a year; they clean them 700 to 800 times. That's why a patient can't skip the deep cleaning even if they'll need surgery: a surgeon treats an infected cut before operating on the broken bone under it, and swollen gum bleeds and tears.

The recheck comes 4 to 6 weeks after Phase I, when the cleaning has had its full effect and home care is at its best. It asks whether the first round of treatment is done (causes controlled, good home care, no plaque or tartar, less inflammation, shallower pockets), whether what's left can be maintained, and whether surgery would help: bone reshaping, regrowing bone, an open-flap cleaning or a gum graft. Three outcomes: shallow pockets and good home care means maintenance every 3 to 4 months; plaque and bleeding everywhere means repeat Phase I; good home care but pockets still too deep for a brush or floss means surgery.

His slides list 11 reasons for gum surgery, led by getting access to clean the roots and getting rid of pockets. A 1981 study he still uses showed that the deeper the pocket, the more tartar a deep cleaning leaves behind: in 3 to 5 mm pockets failure becomes more likely, and over 5 mm it dominates. Deeper pockets have more root to clean, more irregular spots (like furcations), and a narrow bottom you can't reach. Lifting the gum lets you see what you're doing, like doing a filling with your eyes open.

Bone surgery: why remove bone

The goal of osseous surgery is to get rid of pockets and leave a shallow gum collar the patient can keep clean. Healthy gum is scalloped, like a child's drawing of ocean waves: higher between the teeth, lower in the middle of each tooth. It goes back to that shape after surgery even if the bone underneath doesn't. His most important slide: if the bone doesn't follow the shape of the gum above it, the pockets come back. So the surgery reshapes the bone to match. Treating bone loss by removing bone sounds backwards, but sometimes you fight fire with fire.

Gum disease leaves the bone edge uneven. In health, the bone between teeth sits about 1 to 2 mm below the enamel line on an X-ray, and it sits higher than the bone on the cheek and tongue sides, following the curve of the enamel line. That's positive architecture, the goal. In negative (reverse) architecture the bone between the teeth sits lower, making a crater with deep pockets; flat is in between. When getting to positive would mean removing too much bone, he settles for flat rather than weaken the tooth.

The cost is small: about 0.6 mm of supporting bone height on average. Bone comes off the cheek and tongue sides, never between the teeth, because those narrower surfaces hold less of the tooth's support. Teeth feel a bit looser afterward but settle back within about a year.

When to do it, and when not to

Bone surgery fits when the deep cleaning didn't stop the disease; pockets stayed deep after cleaning, especially around furcations; bone loss is mild to moderate and even; there are shallow bone craters or shallow 1-, 2- or 3-wall holes; a shallow furcation needs opening up; or there are bony ledges and bumps (like tori) where the gum meets the tooth at almost a right angle. The aim is bone that tapers to a thin edge at the root, with rounded rather than dented shapes.

It's ruled out by poor home care (the big one; surgery cures nothing, it only makes cleaning possible), a patient who won't follow the plan (like wanting to skip the deep cleaning), shallow pockets (surgery there causes attachment loss), a bone hole that could be regrown instead (Session 6), a result that would look bad (long front teeth with a high smile), and uncontrolled medical disease.

Ostectomy, osteoplasty and the steps

Ostectomy removes bone that supports the tooth (bone the ligament attaches to). Osteoplasty only reshapes bone that isn't attached to the tooth, so it can be thinned more freely. The steps: 1. vertical grooves between the teeth, 2. blending over the roots, 3. flattening the bone between the teeth, and 4. tapering the bone edge, the careful ostectomy on the cheek and tongue sides. The most important step of all is cleaning the roots thoroughly: if the roots aren't clean, nothing works.

On upper molars, each cheek-side root is treated like its own tooth, and the bone in the furcation is never removed: exposing it lowers the outlook, and it's hard to get back. Silk stitches come out after a week. Patients should expect longer-looking teeth, some cold sensitivity on the exposed roots, and wider gaps that catch food but can now be cleaned with a small brush. In his case, a bridge the patient couldn't clean under became cleanable with an interproximal brush six months after surgery, the whole point. But if the patient doesn't clean, none of it works.
plain.periodontal-regeneration:
These notes come from Dr. Geurs' slides, posted before the lecture, plus the class exam-review guide. His two goals for the session: picking the right cases for regeneration, and what regeneration can actually achieve.

What regeneration means

Periodontal regeneration means growing back all three parts of the tooth's attachment: new bone, new cementum (the thin layer on the root) and new periodontal ligament (the fibers that hold the tooth in the bone), so the tooth has a working attachment again, on a root that gum disease had stripped bare. All three have to grow back; more bone on an X-ray isn't enough. The opposite is repair: healing that closes the wound but doesn't rebuild the original structure. After a flap or a deep cleaning, the root usually just repairs: a long strip of gum lining, a long junctional epithelium, sticks to the root instead of new cementum and fibers.

What it takes

Four things have to come together: cells that can build the tissue (from the ligament and bone next to the hole), a scaffold for them to grow into, growth factors that call them in and make them multiply, and a blood supply to feed it all. The slides' map splits the approaches in two. Tissue engineering brings in cells: grown in a lab, clumped together, or seeded onto a scaffold, which can even be 3D printed. Endogenous regeneration adds no cells: it calls the patient's own cells to the spot (cell homing) with growth signals, tissue matrix, tiny cell-made packages called exosomes, or drugs. Everything in this deck's cases is the second kind: grafts, membranes and biologic gels that work with the patient's own cells.

Picking the case: the shape of the defect

Bone holes beside the root (intrabony defects) are sorted by how many bone walls are left around them, how wide they are and how deep they are. One hole often mixes types: three walls at the bottom and fewer near the top. The best ones for regeneration are deeper than 3 mm, with walls at an angle of 25 degrees or less to the root on the X-ray, so narrow rather than wide and shallow. A 2021 review agrees: deeper, narrower defects with more walls gain more attachment and more bone a year after surgery. For example, a 1-wall hole gained about 1.2 mm less bone than a 3-wall hole, and depth was the most reliable predictor. Walls hold the blood clot and graft in place, bring in cells and blood vessels from more sides, and hold up the gum. The exam-review guide says it simply: 3-wall defects are the best candidates.

A defect with mostly one wall is called non-supportive, and it's a big risk for failure. In one 2012 study, a 1-wall defect and thin, scalloped gums were the two things that predicted more gum recession on the front of the tooth after surgery. An X-ray is a flat picture of a 3-D hole; the slides' X-rays of 3-, 2- and 1-wall holes on the same skull molar look surprisingly alike. So you only really count the walls during surgery, once the gum is lifted and the hole is cleaned out.

The risk checklist and the decision tree

A 2023 risk checklist rates each case low, medium or high risk in four areas. The patient: healthy healing or not; smoking (none is low, 10 a day or fewer is medium, more than 10 is high); plaque left on the teeth (15% or less is low, 16 to 24% medium, 25% or more high); showing up for maintenance; and realistic hopes. The tooth: its overall gum risk; whether bite trauma and looseness can be controlled; the nerve (a healthy nerve with the hole not reaching the root tip, or a good root canal, is low; an existing root canal needs a careful look; a hole reaching the root tip, a poor root canal or a dead nerve is high); the root surface (flat is low, dented medium, two fused roots high); healthy gum or not; and gum thickness (thick is low, thin with at least 2 mm of firm gum medium, thin with little or none high). The defect: 3-wall, narrow and deep is low, 2-wall medium, 1-wall, wide and shallow high; no furcation is low, Class I or II medium, Class III high; it must be reachable to clean during surgery (front teeth easiest); and a contained hole, touching 1 or 2 sides of the root, is low, while one touching 3 or more sides is high. The surgeon: experience, stress, and whether they use a checklist.

A decision tree from the AAP Regeneration Workshop says what to do. First, fix the patient: uncontrolled medical problems, smoking and other habits, and poor cleaning at home. Then, after the first round of treatment, check the pockets, bleeding, looseness, the bone and any other dental work. A bone hole under 3 mm isn't a regeneration case: pockets of 5 mm or less without bleeding get non-surgical care; deeper pockets get bone-reshaping surgery. For a hole 3 mm or deeper, the best odds go 3-wall, then circumferential or 2-wall, then 1-wall, and narrow beats wide. If the tooth's outlook is poor, it comes out and gets replaced. Otherwise the hole decides the treatment: a narrow 3-wall or circumferential hole (under 2 mm wide) gets a bone graft, a membrane or a biologic; a wide one (3 mm or more) or a 2-wall hole gets a reinforced membrane, a graft plus a membrane, or a graft plus a biologic; a 1-wall hole gets combination therapy or a bone graft that contains living cells. Looks matter too: if the patient shows a lot of gum when smiling, has thin gums or has lost the gum between the teeth, go ahead only if they accept the risk to looks, skip the membrane, and think about a gum graft.

The toolbox

Regeneration aims to regrow bone, cementum and ligament and gain attachment, mainly in 2- and 3-wall bone holes. The slides list bone grafts, guided tissue regeneration (GTR), combination therapy, biologics such as enamel matrix proteins or PDGF, and MIST, a minimally invasive surgery done through a small flap that keeps the gum between the teeth. Regeneration rebuilds lost support; resective surgery from Session 5 does the opposite and reshapes the bone to get rid of the pocket.

Bone grafts. The slides' graft case used DFDBA (demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft): donor bone from a tissue bank. The hole was filled, and after healing the pocket measured 3 mm. Grafts are named by where they come from: autograft, from the patient; allograft, from another person; xenograft, from an animal, such as cow bone; and alloplast, a man-made material such as beta-tricalcium phosphate.

Guided tissue regeneration. A thin barrier membrane goes over the hole, under the gum. Gum tissue grows much faster than bone and ligament, so the membrane keeps it off the root and gives the slower ligament and bone cells time to fill in. In combination therapy, a bone graft goes under the membrane to hold the space open so the membrane can't sag into the hole. The slides follow these cases on X-rays at 1 year, 20 years and 25 years, and the new bone was still there decades later.

Biologics. Enamel matrix derivative (EMD) is a gel made from the proteins that build enamel and the tooth's attachment while the tooth develops, mostly amelogenins. Alone or with a graft, it works about as well as GTR; the slides show a case healing with it from 2022 to 2025. rhPDGF-BB is a lab-made growth factor that calls in bone and ligament cells, makes them multiply and helps new blood vessels grow. A beta-TCP scaffold is a bone-friendly framework that keeps the gum from collapsing into the hole and holds the clot steady; the exam-review guide pairs it with rhPDGF-BB.

Defects without walls. When a defect has no walls to contain it, nothing holds up the gum or the clot, so a biologic gel alone has no space to work in. These defects usually get a graft too, to support the gum, which is why the decision tree sends a 1-wall hole to combination therapy. The slides follow one such case from the first X-ray through surgery, grafting and stitches to the follow-up X-ray.

What can you achieve?

The starting point is open flap debridement: lifting the gum and cleaning the root, with no graft. In the studies on the slide, pockets of about 7 mm came down to about 4 mm, with about 1.5 mm of attachment gained and about 1 mm of bone. The pocket shrank by 3 mm but the attachment improved by only 1.5 mm, because the rest is the gum shrinking down the root (recession). Regenerative treatments are judged by how much better they do than this. The slides show four mixes healing on X-rays over 3 to 16 months: Emdogain with donor bone, a membrane with the patient's own bone, rhPDGF with donor bone, and donor bone alone.

Proving it worked

There are three ways to check: histology (looking at the tissue under a microscope), clinical measurements (probing) and X-rays. Only histology can show new cementum, new ligament fibers and new bone, so only histology proves real regeneration. A probe can't tell new attachment from a long strip of gum lining stuck to the root, and an X-ray shows bone, not attachment. Subtraction radiography lines up two matching X-rays taken at different times and subtracts one from the other, so only the change shows. Dr. Geurs and colleagues used it in 1996 to test a membrane that dissolves on its own: the new bone lit up on the subtraction image, and under the microscope, 6 months later, new cementum, ligament and bone had grown into a small marker notch cut in the root.
plain.implants-perio:
Dr. Kaur taught this session in class on Oct 29, with her slides. Her question: should people who have had gum disease (periodontitis) get implants? Her answer: yes, once the gum disease is treated, under control, and the patient keeps up with care. Along the way she showed how to tell a healthy implant from a sick one, the same way you already tell healthy gums from gingivitis and periodontitis.

Success versus survival

An implant that survives is just still there and has a crown on it. It can still have problems: inflamed gums around it, bone loss, a broken or loose part, pain or gum shrinking back. A successful implant has no problems at all. Research papers use both words, so check which one they mean.

The success rules on her slide are Albrektsson's from 1986: the implant doesn't move, there's no dark ring around it on the X-ray, there's no pain, infection, numbness or nerve trouble, and it has lost 1.5 mm of bone or less after its first year of use. In class she added: after that first year, no more than 0.2 mm a year. A dark area at the tip of the implant is called retrograde peri-implantitis.

Healthy, inflamed, diseased: the 2017 names

In 2017 an expert workshop gave names to the states around an implant: peri-implant health, peri-implant mucositis (gum inflammation only), peri-implantitis (inflammation plus bone loss), and soft and hard tissue deficiency (gum and bone both lost).

Health. No redness or swelling, no bleeding or pus when you probe gently, no deeper reading than at earlier visits, and no bone loss beyond the normal settling after the implant goes in. There's no 3 mm limit: a healthy implant can probe deeper than 3 mm, depending on how deep it was placed, how tall the connecting piece is, and how thick the gum is. Probing implants accurately is hard, even with a plastic probe. So you always compare an implant with its own starting records, and you have to take those records at the start.

Normal settling. Once an implant starts chewing, the bone at its top reshapes. In class she said about 2 mm, and it levels off within about the first year. That's normal. Any bone loss past that is disease.

Peri-implant mucositis is like gingivitis around an implant: redness and swelling, heavy bleeding (a line or a drop) and/or pus when probed gently, a deeper reading than at the start, but no extra bone loss. The pocket is deeper only because the gum is swollen. It can be reversed, so treat it, don't just watch it. A pocket reading goes up for only three reasons: a measuring mistake, swollen gum, or real bone loss.

Pus means the disease is active right now, at a tooth or an implant, and you have to do something that day: clean the area, and sometimes put an antibiotic into a deep pocket (Session 8).

Peri-implantitis has all the signs of inflammation plus bone loss beyond the normal settling. When you hear the word, picture real bone loss. The official definition: a disease caused by plaque, with inflamed gums around the implant followed by ongoing bone loss. That's why you stop it while it's still only mucositis.

It's hard to fix. In theory only bone has to grow back (implants have no ligament or root surface to rebuild). The trouble is the implant surface: it's made rough on purpose so bone grabs it, and plaque grabs it too. Nothing cleans it better than anything else: salt water, chlorhexidine, citric acid, EDTA and lasers all work about the same. The bone holes around implants are usually not the narrow, deep shape that heals best, and the disease often comes back. A site with an 8-9 mm pocket, pus and bone loss but with bone still standing on the sides and the tongue side can still be treated: open it, clean it, add a growth factor or bone graft, cover it with a membrane and close.

Soft and hard tissue deficiency means the gum is lost along with the bone under it. Thin gum shrinks back faster than thick gum.

Ailing, failing, failed (Meffert 1992)

Ailing: bone was lost but the loss has stopped; no inflammation and the implant doesn't move. Watch it and record it at every visit. Failing: bone loss is still going on and the gum is inflamed, but the implant doesn't move; what to do depends on the case. Failed: bone loss, the implant moves, and it no longer works. A moving implant has lost its bond to the bone (osseointegration), which can never be undone, so it has to come out. First make sure it's the implant itself that moves, not just the connector or the crown.

Peri-implantitis rarely makes an implant loose, even with two-thirds of its bone gone. An implant with bone loss that bad still counts as failed if it has no future.

What causes it

Many things add up, but the cause is plaque bacteria, and they're the same bad bacteria as in gum disease. Risk factors come from the patient, the surgery and implant, the gum, and the crown.

Risk factors for mucositis: smoking (now or in the past), past gum disease, active gum disease, thin gum, and obesity or metabolic syndrome. Risk factors for peri-implantitis: smoking, past or active gum disease, obesity or metabolic syndrome, an implant in the wrong position, poorly controlled diabetes, too little bone width, and depression or antidepressants. Poor brushing and flossing raised the odds about 14 times in one study.

Germs. The bacteria in the mouth before the implant goes in decide which bacteria live around it. Around healthy implants, the bacteria look like those under healthy gums. Genes matter too. A coating from saliva (the pellicle) forms on an implant within 30 minutes of it being exposed. The first settlers are harmless round and rod-shaped bacteria (gram-positive, including Actinomyces); later the gum-disease bacteria move in (P. gingivalis, P. intermedia).

Why it matters how the teeth were lost

Someone who lost teeth to gum disease is a susceptible host, with a higher risk of implant disease, even with no teeth left. Gum-disease bacteria can hang around a year or more after the teeth are pulled. So untreated gum disease rules implants out, but someone whose gum disease is treated and kept under control can have implants, with closer check-ups.

Do things in order: deep cleaning first; pull hopeless teeth but don't put implants in yet; let things heal and teach good home care; re-check; do any gum surgery; and only then plan implants. Check the risks again at each step.

One or two surgeries. In a two-stage implant, a cap goes on and the gum is closed over it; about 3-4 months later it's uncovered, a healing post that sticks through the gum goes on, and 2-3 weeks later the impression is taken. In a single-stage implant the healing post goes on the same day.

The #31 case. A 41-year-old man with untreated gum disease got an implant at #31 with a bone graft next to #30, then never came back for care. Two years later his only complaint was food getting stuck. Gum and bone were both gone around #31. The implant was unscrewed and removed, #30 was also pulled, the bone was rebuilt in height, and two new implants went in. A gentler option would have been a root canal on #30 and removing only its bad root.

A 2006 European consensus found more peri-implantitis and more bone loss in people who lost teeth to gum disease, and a 10-year study found that people with gum disease lost more implants.

The challenges

Gum loss: missing papillae, black triangles and less firm (keratinized) gum, worse with thin gum. Both how much firm gum there is and how thick it is matter, most of all in the smile zone.

Bone loss: an implant in short bone carries a long crown, and that can break the implant. Growing bone wider is much easier than growing it taller. A sinus lift is the easy kind of taller, since the bone grows up into the sinus. In one patient missing #1-7, the bone was too short, the front implants were lost, and he ended up with a removable denture on the remaining implants.

Ways to add bone: grafting a socket, building up the ridge, sinus lifts; moving the nerve or using short implants; and distraction osteogenesis (slowly stretching bone to make it taller).

Checking risk at every step

Check the risks before the implant goes in, while it heals into the bone, at every maintenance visit, and after an implant is removed. Anything that raises the risk of gum disease also raises the risk of implant failure.

Smoking hurts three ways. Germs: smokers carry nastier bacteria that are harder to clear (A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis, B. forsythus), and smoke lowers oxygen, which those bacteria like. Immune system: white cells move and eat bacteria poorly, there are fewer helper T cells and B cells, and more inflammatory signals (IL-6, TNF-alpha) and tissue-breaking collagenase. Healing: nicotine slows new blood vessel growth. In one study of 2,194 implants, 11.3% failed in smokers vs 4.76% in nonsmokers; heavier smokers do worse (the more you smoke, the worse it gets); and peri-implantitis hit 23.5% of smokers vs 16.5% of nonsmokers. Risk starts below a pack a day. Vaping hasn't been studied long; it may not squeeze blood vessels the way smoke does, but it still weakens the immune response.

Diabetes. How long someone has had diabetes doesn't matter if it's well controlled. Poorly controlled diabetes rules implants out. Control is measured with HbA1c, which shows the last 3-4 months because that's how long red blood cells live. (Outside the lecture: UAB's clinic says no to implants at an HbA1c of 8 or higher.)

From the exam-review guide: some people carry IL-1 gene variants that make them overreact to bacteria, and that gene plus smoking raises peri-implantitis risk more than the two would add up to.

Check-ups: probing, bleeding and X-rays

Implants are checked with plastic implant probes and cleaned with implant scalers. At each visit look at: bleeding when probed lightly (about 0.25 N), the gum, pus, pocket depth, pain, movement and bone loss on X-ray.

Bleeding can come from probing too hard or at the wrong angle, or from inflamed gum. No bleeding is a good sign that the implant is stable. Bleeding means inflammation but doesn't prove the disease is getting worse. A little slow bleeding may be nothing; heavy bleeding that fills the pocket is a warning. Follow it over time: a site that bled at all 4 visits had a 30% chance of losing attachment, 3 of 4 visits 14%, 2 of 4 6%, 1 of 4 3%, and never 1.5%.

X-rays are taken when the implant goes in, before it's uncovered (or before the crown work if it's one surgery), at the final impression, when the final connector goes on, and when the final crown goes on (the starting X-ray); then every 6 months in the first year, then once a year. Take an extra one only when probing shows a change (deeper pocket, bleeding, pus): X-rays confirm what you found, they're not for fishing.

Bottom line

Checking and controlling risk is part of implant care. Tell patients with past gum disease that their risk is higher. Treat gum disease before placing implants. Good home care and regular check-ups decide the outcome, so make the patient your partner. A patient whose gum disease is treated, stable and who keeps up with care can have implants.
plain.antibiotics-host-mod:
Dr. Litz taught this in two parts: he recorded the antibiotics half (the file is from March 2024; he gives the same lecture every year), then taught host modulation in class on Nov 5, after a quick antibiotics recap. He kept only what you need when you start treating patients.

Bacteria cause it, but antibiotics are only for some cases

Gum disease is started by a small group of bacteria that normally live in the mouth, mostly gram-negative, oxygen-hating rods living in a biofilm. If an exam asks what causes gum disease, the answer is bacteria and plaque ("don't even look at the other answers"). Smoking and diabetes make it worse, but without bacteria there's no gum or bone loss. Since it's an infection, antibiotics can help, but only in certain cases.

Gum treatment starts with Phase I, the non-surgical part: first teaching home care (he calls it the most important visit, because nothing lasts if the patient can't keep their teeth clean), then deep cleaning (scaling and root planing), then, if needed, drugs. If antibiotics are used, they come after the deep cleaning.

When antibiotics are considered: an infection that's spreading, with fever, feeling sick, or swollen glands; aggressive periodontitis, fast, severe gum disease in young people; and refractory periodontitis, gum disease that keeps getting worse even though the patient and dentist did everything right. And always as an add-on to cleaning or surgery, never by themselves. That's his main point.

Why pills alone don't work: biofilm

The bacteria live in a biofilm: many kinds of germs living together in a protective bubble (if one colony is a house, a biofilm is a whole neighborhood). Biofilm is sticky and won't dissolve, so rinses, water flossers and mouthwash don't remove it, just like a dirty pot left to soak still has to be scrubbed. The scrubbing is mechanical cleaning: the patient's brush and floss, and our scalers. Some biofilm germs survive drug levels 500-1000 times higher than a pill can reach. He called this one to know for life: only mechanical cleaning removes biofilm.

Biofilm protects germs from antibiotics three ways: (1) it's a wall the drug can't get through; (2) it's full of beta-lactamase, an enzyme that destroys our strongest antibiotics; and (3) it slows the germs' growth, which makes many antibiotics work worse.

A pill's drug spreads through the whole body, not just to the sick gum. Some reaches the gum fluid, but not enough to kill germs in a biofilm unless the biofilm is cleaned off first. Clean first, then add the antibiotic.

Killers and stoppers

Bacteriostatic drugs stop germs from growing and let the body finish them off. Bactericidal drugs kill germs, but only germs that are actively dividing. So if two antibiotics are given together, they must be both killers or both stoppers: a stopper would slow the germs down and leave the killer nothing to work on.

Amoxicillin, and writing a prescription

Amoxicillin is a penicillin that covers both gram-negative and gram-positive germs and kills them by blocking their cell walls. It's used for aggressive periodontitis. Beta-lactamase can destroy it. Dose: 500 mg by mouth three times a day for 7 days (some use 875 mg twice a day: fewer pills, so patients are more likely to take them all).

Short forms: po = by mouth, qd = once a day, bid = twice, tid = three times, qid = four times. A prescription needs the drug and strength, how many to give (21 tablets for three a day for a week), and how to take it, plus the patient's details, the date, your details, refills and your signature.

Allergy is the most common problem: about 10-15% of adults are allergic to penicillin. Always ask before prescribing. If they say they're allergic, ask what happens: an upset stomach is a side effect, not an allergy. Hives or trouble breathing mean a true, possibly deadly allergy: no drug from that family.

Almost all antibiotics can make birth control pills work less well and can make Coumadin (warfarin), a blood thinner, too strong: they kill gut bacteria that make vitamin K, which normally blunts warfarin. You can still prescribe; just tell the patient's physician and let them decide about the warfarin. Never change another doctor's prescription yourself.

Augmentin and cephalosporins

Augmentin is amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid, which blocks beta-lactamase so the amoxicillin can work. It's for aggressive or stubborn gum disease. It upsets the stomach more (take it with food) and costs more. The clavulanic acid is always 125 mg.

Cephalosporins work like penicillins (they kill by blocking cell walls). Newer generations cover more gram-negative germs and resist beta-lactamase better. They may reach bone better and can be taken with food. About 1 in 10 people allergic to penicillin also react to them, so don't give one if the patient is allergic to penicillin and unsure about cephalosporins. As taught, someone allergic to cephalosporins should be treated as allergic to penicillin too.

Clindamycin

Clindamycin blocks the 50S part of the bacterial ribosome (the machine that makes proteins) and usually kills germs. It's the usual pick when a patient is truly allergic to penicillins and cephalosporins: 150-300 mg three times a day for 7 days. Its danger is C. diff colitis: it wipes out good gut bacteria and lets C. diff overgrow, which can be deadly. Don't give it to someone who has had colitis.

Tetracyclines

Tetracycline stops growth by blocking the 30S part of the ribosome and covers many germs, but decades of use have made many germs resistant, so it works worse than penicillins. It may be used when A. actinomycetemcomitans is the main germ (localized aggressive periodontitis). Problems: upset stomach (most common), longer bleeding, staining and weak enamel in developing teeth (so not in pregnancy or under age 8), sunburn easily, and calcium, magnesium, iron and aluminum block its absorption: no milk, dairy, iron pills or antacids, and take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals.

Doxycycline and minocycline are newer versions that absorb better and upset the stomach less. Doxycycline: 100 mg once a day. Minocycline: 100 mg twice a day. A tiny dose of doxycycline (20 mg twice a day) is used to block tissue-breaking enzymes (Periostat, below).

Macrolides

Erythromycin, azithromycin and clarithromycin block the 50S part of the ribosome and stop growth. Azithromycin and clarithromycin cover oxygen-hating germs better than erythromycin. Erythromycin isn't recommended for gum disease: too many germs resist it, and nearly everyone gets an upset stomach. Azithromycin (Z-Pak): 500 mg on day 1, then 250 mg on days 2-5; food lowers its absorption, so take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals. Clarithromycin: fine with or without food, but avoid it in pregnancy (pregnancy category C). Macrolides can raise levels of other drugs, especially the heart drug digoxin, and also warfarin, Dilantin, cyclosporine, midazolam, steroids and theophylline. (His story: Van Gogh's Starry Night halos may come from too much digoxin.)

Metronidazole

Works only on germs that can't live with oxygen, especially spirochetes. It damages bacterial DNA and kills them. Used for aggressive periodontitis and ANUG (a painful, fast gum infection), often together with amoxicillin (both killers). 250 mg three times a day. It makes warfarin stronger, can raise lithium levels, and can harm a fetus. Tell every patient: urine may turn orange-red, and no alcohol, or they'll get a terrible headache.

Ciprofloxacin

Cipro kills germs by blocking the enzyme that untwists their DNA (DNA gyrase). It covers gram-negative germs, but oxygen-hating germs mostly resist it, and those are the gum-disease germs. It absorbs fastest 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals, can cause sun reactions, and affects theophylline, caffeine and warfarin. It's given with metronidazole to cover the germs it misses, and only far down the list.

The dose chart: know it for the exam

In class he said to know the doses: "I would know this for the exam." His chart's usual adult doses, and how long to take them:

  • Augmentin (amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid): 250 or 500 mg three times a day for 10 days.
  • Amoxicillin plus metronidazole: 375 mg amoxicillin and 250 mg metronidazole, each three times a day, for 7 days.
  • Clindamycin: 150-300 mg four times a day for 10 days.
  • Doxycycline: 100 mg twice on the first day, then 100 mg a day, for 10-14 days.
  • Metronidazole: 250 mg three or four times a day for 10 days.
  • Minocycline: 200 mg twice on the first day, then 100 mg twice a day, for 10-14 days.
  • Tetracycline: 250 mg four times a day for 14-21 days, the longest on the chart.

The two with metronidazole aren't for children under 16, and the tetracycline family is dosed for children only over 8. A few doses differ from the drug-by-drug slides, so know both: clindamycin's slide says three times a day for 7 days, doxycycline's says 100 mg once a day, and Augmentin is usually written as 500 or 875 mg.

Side effects of antibiotic pills

Upset stomach and diarrhea, overgrowth of harmful germs like C. diff, weaker birth control, and more bleeding with blood thinners. To help: yogurt or buttermilk with live cultures, and an antifungal (nystatin, or one Diflucan pill at the start) for patients who get yeast infections.

Drugs placed in the pocket

These go into the pocket right after deep cleaning, once the biofilm is broken up. They put a high dose right where it's needed for a long time, which also lowers the chance of resistance. They can't fix the bone damage the disease already caused.

When to use them: one problem spot in a patient whose gums are otherwise stable (a site that was 3 mm for years is now 5 mm and bleeding). Numb it, clean it, place the drug, and re-check in 4-6 weeks. Many deep pockets after Phase I need surgery instead. Not a replacement for cleaning, and not for aggressive periodontitis.

PerioChip: 2.5 mg of chlorhexidine in a small gelatin chip that sticks when wet and dissolves on its own. The drug peaks about 2 hours after placing it and tapers off over about 9 days.

Atridox: 10% doxycycline gel made by linking two syringes and mixing back and forth about 100 times (1½ minutes). It hardens in the pocket and dissolves over a few weeks. No brushing, flossing or eating at that spot for 7 days.

Arestin: 1 mg of minocycline in tiny beads, squeezed into the pocket from a cartridge while pulling the tip out. It sticks when wet, dissolves on its own, and keeps working about 14 days. No brushing the spot for 12 hours and no flossing it for 10 days.

Host modulation: what it means

Dr. Litz taught this part in class. The host is the person the germs live on: your patient with plaque. Modulation means changing how something works in response to a trigger. So host modulation asks: can we change how the patient's body reacts to the gum germs, the reaction that causes gum and bone loss? It's taught with antibiotics because the answer involves drugs, an antibiotic among them.

Germs are the key; the body's reaction is the engine

Gum disease can't start or get worse without gram-negative bacteria; they're the main cause. But they're not enough on their own. He said to know this point: most of the damage comes from the body's own reaction to the germs. The deep pockets, and the bone loss on x-rays, come largely from the way our body fights the bacteria.

It goes in a chain: germs build up at the gumline, the body sees them as invaders and sends cells to fight, those cells release inflammation signals (cytokines and prostaglandins), and as collateral damage the signals break down gum fibers and bone, which shows up as deeper pockets and bone loss. A deeper pocket holds more germs, more germs call in more cells and more signals, and the damage grows: a vicious cycle.

But it always starts with the germs. Gum disease is not an autoimmune disease: the body doesn't attack itself for no reason. His picture is a car in your garage. The engine (the body's reaction) is what moves you from healthy gums to gum disease, but it won't start by itself in the middle of the night. It needs the key, and the key is the germs.

What happens in the gum

The germs: a thin saliva coating forms within minutes of a cleaning, before the patient even leaves the office, and germs stick to it. The first settlers are harmless gram-positive cocci that feed on proteins in saliva. If brushing slips, plaque at the gumline makes the gum inflamed, and that lets the nastier late germs (the orange and red complexes) move in; they feed on blood and gum fluid. The germs arrive in a set order, and the biofilm shelters them.

The body's defense: first come complement proteins from the blood. They can burst germs, but their main job is to call in white cells, and they make mast cells release histamine, which makes blood vessels leaky, so the gum swells. Neutrophils are the first responders, like paramedics, arriving within about 1-2 days; if they can't win, macrophages come later. Both are good cells we can't live without, but both release cytokines, signals between cells.

One cytokine, IL-1, is also called osteoclast activating factor: it switches on the bone-eating cells (osteoclasts), turns up collagenase (which breaks down gum fibers) and PGE2, and all of that releases MMPs (tissue-eating enzymes). Germs can damage tissue directly too, but how bad the loss gets depends mostly on the body's own cells. The body's reaction may be the biggest single factor in how severe the disease gets, how fast it moves, and how well it responds to treatment.

Turning the reaction down, carefully

Deep cleaning lowers the germ load, but it never removes every germ, especially in deep pockets and furcations. Host modulation therapy tries to turn down the destructive part of the reaction and turn up the protective part, alongside regular treatment, so the balance tips toward healing.

He warned to be careful: turn someone's defenses down too far and a small infection could become serious, even deadly. Medicine already does this for arthritis and osteoporosis; dentistry started in the 1990s (Williams and Golub, 1990).

NSAIDs

NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen) block PGE2, which turns on bone breakdown. Taken every day for up to 3 years, they slowed bone loss, but they only help if taken every day, and long-term use can cause stomach problems and ulcers, bleeding (platelets stick together less), and kidney or liver harm. So they aren't used this way.

Bisphosphonates

Bisphosphonates (common osteoporosis drugs, mostly for older women) slow the bone-eating cells. The problem is jawbone death (BRONJ) after an extraction or gum surgery, sometimes on its own, mostly with strong IV doses. It looks like an infection but isn't: the gum pulls back and the bone underneath dies. Treating it means scraping off the dead bone, but scraping is injury, the very thing that causes it, so the spot can come back bigger. These drugs stay in the body for years. Because of this, none is approved for gum disease.

Periostat

Periostat is doxycycline at a dose too low to kill germs: 20 mg twice a day, a fifth of the 100 mg antibiotic dose. It's the first FDA-approved pill for host modulation, used with deep cleaning. It blocks collagenase, the tissue-breaking enzyme made by the body's own white cells. The germs aren't affected, so they don't become resistant, and it can be taken long-term. Take it away from meals and calcium. Not for people allergic to tetracyclines, pregnant or nursing women, or children under 12.

In Caton's 2000 study, patients got the same deep cleaning, then took either Periostat or a dummy pill for 9 months. Periostat gave more pocket shrinkage and attachment gain at 3, 6 and 9 months, enough to be statistically real, but only fractions of a millimeter. Don't memorize the numbers; know the point: real but small, and most useful for stubborn (refractory) and aggressive cases. Nobody has shown it works past 9 months or is safe past 12, and it never replaces cleaning and good home care.

Controlling germs comes first. Periostat can be considered for people with risks that are hard to change, like smoking or diabetes, if they take it twice a day, keep brushing and flossing well, and keep coming to their gum check-ups. A pill isn't a magic cure.

Bottom line

Deep cleaning alone works. He said to definitely know this one: antibiotics alone don't, and they're never the first step. Added to cleaning, they can help a bit, in select cases: aggressive periodontitis, refractory periodontitis, and a few problem spots in maintenance patients. Treat the cause, not just the symptoms. His references: the Drug Information Handbook for Dentistry, the free Epocrates app, and the Little Dental Drug Booklet, which has common dental prescriptions written out.
plain.perio-plastic-esthetics:
Dr. Abou-Arraj taught this in two parts. He recorded the first part (posted Nov 9): gum thickness, receding gums and how they're grafted, missing firm gum, and the frenum. The last two problems, too much gum and gum discoloration, he covers in a live class the week of Nov 9. Until that class is posted, those parts come from his slides and the class exam-review guide.

The tissues

The mucogingival junction (MGJ) is the line between the firm, pink gum (gingiva) and the loose, redder lining of the mouth (alveolar mucosa). You can often see it, but a probe finds it best. All the gum above that line is keratinized gingiva, the tough kind. Part of it is stuck down to the tooth and bone (attached gingiva); the edge is free (free gingiva), and that's where the probe slips in to measure pocket depth.

Gum and lining problems

Periodontal plastic therapy fixes mucogingival deformities: anything abnormal about the amount, size, outline or shape of the soft tissue around teeth. The current classification (the 2017 World Workshop) lists seven: (1) gum thickness and shape (the phenotype); (2) receding gums (recession); (3) not enough firm gum (lack of keratinized gingiva); (4) a shallow vestibule; (5) a frenum or muscle attached too high; (6) too much gum (gingival excess); and (7) discolored gum (a tattoo).

Thin or thick gums

The phenotype is how thick the gum is (thin or thick) and how its edge is shaped (scalloped or flat). To test thickness, put the probe in the pocket. If you can see the probe through the gum, it's thin, 1 mm or less. If you can't, it's thick, more than 1 mm.

It matters because thin gum recedes more easily, and recession on thin gum tends to get worse; thick gum resists it. His example: a young patient with gum so thin you could see the roots was about to get braces. Braces plus years of brushing could make his gums recede, so before the braces the gum was made thicker: a flap was lifted, a piece of connective tissue from the palate was stitched over the two front teeth most at risk, and the flap was laid back over it. Two weeks later the gum was already thicker, and he went ahead with braces.

Receding gums: what and who

Recession means the gum edge has moved below the CEJ (where the enamel ends), so some root shows. Measure it from the gum edge to the CEJ at the same six spots as pocket depth. Check between the teeth too, because recession there changes what treatment can do.

It's very common. The slide: 88% of people 65 and over and 50% of people 18 to 64 have at least one spot. In the recording: over half of Americans 30 and older have at least 1 mm, and almost a quarter have at least one spot of 3 mm or more. Older people have more because they've piled up more risk factors over the years, not because of age itself. It's more common in men and in African-Americans, and most common on the cheek side of upper molars (especially first molars) and lower front teeth; canines are common too.

What sets it up

The slide's list of ten: gum disease (periodontitis); injury (brushing, flossing, picking, objects); bone variations (a window or a gap in the bone over the root) and teeth out of line; not enough firm gum; thin gum; braces; past gum surgery; a frenum or muscle attached high; filling and crown edges; and chewing tobacco. What he added:

Gum disease means periodontitis, not gingivitis: losing bone and attachment uncovers the root. Past gum surgery: resective surgery causes most of its recession on purpose, to leave no pockets, so the patient can keep the area clean. Brushing is the most common injury: hard bristles, or simply brushing too hard. Flossing habits, picking, objects like a fingernail or pen, and harsh medicines put right on the gum count too.

Bone variations. A fenestration is a window in the bone over the root; a dehiscence is missing bone from the top edge down. A tooth that sits out toward the cheek has thinner gum and gets hit harder by the brush. Moving it back into line with braces can undo some recession without a graft. Thin gum plus missing bone plus hard brushing is "the perfect storm."

Braces that push teeth out of their bone over thin gum can cause recession, though some studies disagree; he calls it controversial. Crown and filling edges placed under the gum, poorly fitting, or too bulky on thin gum can cause it (not that every crown needs a graft). A high frenum tugs on the gum edge with every movement. Chewing tobacco, held in one spot, usually the lower back teeth, can cause severe recession right there; his worst case had recession down to the bottom of the vestibule, with no pockets.

How it happens

Two ways. Brushing injury, especially on thin gum: the surface is scraped, the tissue underneath gets inflamed, a small sore forms, and with more injury the gum edge pulls back. Plaque: the same process as periodontitis, plaque left in the pocket causing attachment loss, just in one small spot on thin gum. Either way, his key word is inflammation: it's what actually causes recession. Everything on the list just sets it up.

The Cairo grades: how much root can be covered?

Before suggesting a graft, grade the recession, because the grade predicts the result. The Cairo system has three:

RT1: no attachment lost between the teeth; you can't find the CEJ between the teeth. The best case: about 100% of the root can be covered.

RT2: some attachment lost between the teeth, but no more than on the front of the tooth (the attachment loss between the teeth is less than or equal to the loss on the cheek side). You can see the CEJ between the teeth. Expect partial coverage, about 50 to 60% in his examples: only up to the level of the attachment between the teeth, because there's nothing there to hold the gum higher and no blood supply for it.

RT3: more attachment lost between the teeth than on the front. A graft won't cover the root at all, so don't try for coverage.

Why treat it

Exposed roots and lost tissue make these more likely: (1) sensitive teeth, (2) sore gums (thin gum can hurt to brush), (3) root cavities, (4) looks, (5) harder cleaning, and (6) the gum inflames more easily. And it keeps going: a 2016 review (Chambrone and Tatakis) found untreated recession keeps getting worse. So "it doesn't hurt, let's just watch it" doesn't mean it will stay the same. Except for RT3, consider treating it when there's a reason to. (Fixing recession with fillings is next year's course.)

Gum grafts: where they come from

Two main sources: the patient's own tissue (an autograft) and donor tissue from a tissue bank (an allograft). Animal sources exist too. The most common graft comes from the palate, because palate tissue is the tough, keratinized kind, and its connective tissue teaches the new site to grow tough gum. Two kinds come from the palate: a free gingival graft (FGG), the surface layer plus the connective tissue in one piece; and a connective tissue graft (CTG), only the connective tissue, no surface layer.

The palate's layers, from the surface down: a thin surface layer (0.3-0.6 mm), the thick connective tissue (1.25-3 mm), then fat and glands, then bone. A thick graft brings fat along, and that's trimmed off so it doesn't slow healing.

Stay away from the big artery and nerve of the palate (the greater palatine). On the slide it sits about 7 mm from the CEJ in a shallow palate, 12 mm in an average one and 17 mm in a high one. So a high, deep palate gives the most room for error.

A CTG can be taken two ways: open a trap door and take the connective tissue from underneath, or cut out the whole piece with its surface layer and peel the surface layer off after. The exam-review guide's version: sometimes an FGG is cut but used as a CTG, because that's easier.

The rule: if a flap will cover the graft, use connective tissue only, because surface layer pressed against the flap's underside won't heal. If the graft will be left uncovered, use an FGG.

Covering a root: CTG under a flap pulled up

His case: recession on #10 and #11. He lifted a flap, took a CTG from the palate, stitched it over the roots, and pulled the flap up over it (a coronally advanced flap), with no tension so it stays put. Four weeks later the roots were well covered, and the gum over them was much thicker, which resists more recession. His rule: "We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft."

Many teeth: donor skin

Grafting many teeth from the palate means a big, painful harvest. Instead, use an allograft: donated human skin (dermis), cleaned of its surface layer, hair follicles and cells, leaving a framework of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers. This is acellular dermal matrix (ADM), the most common donor graft (AlloDerm is one). It was made for burns and reconstructions (since 1995) and used in dentistry since 1997.

Pros: no second wound on the palate, patients accept it more, shorter surgery, many teeth at once, good-looking results, easy to use. Cons: it's "more or less a dead piece of skin," like a band-aid, with nothing alive to help healing. So it must be completely covered by the flap; over time the body replaces it with its own tissue. In a tough site it can't match the patient's own tissue (the guide: it doesn't work as well as an autograft, but has many advantages).

His case: five or six teeth, canine to canine, with RT2 and RT3 recession. He used a tunnel flap: like an envelope, but without lifting the gum between the teeth, joining the pockets of all the teeth into one tunnel under the gum. The ADM was soaked in two baths (the second with the antibiotic tetracycline), slid into the tunnel, held with sling stitches, and covered by pulling the flap up. Six months later it was a good result for that starting point.

Not enough firm gum

Keratinized gingiva (KG) is measured from the gum edge to the MGJ. To find the MGJ, look for the color change, or roll the probe up from the loose lining: the lining rolls with it, and where it stops rolling is the MGJ.

On average the upper front teeth have the most, the canine and first premolar the least, and the molars more again; the lower arch is similar, and on the tongue side of the lower jaw the front teeth have the least.

Do you need it? With good plaque control and no other injury, a band of attached gum isn't essential for healthy gums. But if plaque control isn't great, at least 2 mm of KG is needed to prevent attachment loss. Many patients don't clean perfectly, so a tooth with under 2 mm is likely to recede. Still, it's case by case: not every such tooth needs a graft.

Growing firm gum: an FGG left uncovered

His patient had RT2 recession, a sensitive tooth and no firm gum, so the spot trapped plaque and kept receding. The goal was a band of firm gum, with any root coverage a bonus. A CTG under a flap wouldn't help: the only tissue to cover it with was loose lining, and lining doesn't turn into firm gum by covering a graft. So he did an FGG: the flap was moved down (an apically positioned flap), and a graft with its surface layer was stitched on and left uncovered, so it heals into firm gum. The palate wound heals on its own (secondary intention). The graft is held only by stitches, so the patient shouldn't pull the lip to look at it, should eat soft food and shouldn't brush there while it heals. Three months later: a good band of firm gum, some root coverage (as expected for RT2), no more sensitivity, and a spot that's easier to clean.

The frenum

A frenum attached too high pulls on the gum edge every time the lip and face move, which traps plaque and makes recession worse. In one patient it was in the way of her new crowns looking good, so it was removed before the final crowns (a frenectomy): cut out the frenum in a diamond shape and close it with a few stitches into the lip.

Too much gum (slides; the live class)

Four causes, each with its fix. 1. Pseudopocket: swollen gums from gingivitis make the pocket deeper without any attachment loss. Fix: better home care and a cleaning. 2. Overgrowth from a drug: phenytoin (a seizure drug), calcium channel blockers (blood pressure drugs) and cyclosporine. Fix: cut away the extra gum (gingivectomy), better home care, and maybe change the drug. 3. Uneven gum lines between matching teeth. Fix: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap. 4. A gummy smile. Fix: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap, once you know the cause.

Gummy smile: find the cause

Each cause has a sign on the slides: short teeth (altered passive eruption), with odd tooth sizes and proportions and uneven gum lines; an upper jaw grown too far down (vertical maxillary excess), with a long lower third of the face; a short upper lip, under 20 mm; a lip that lifts too far, more than 8 mm; or a mix.

Gum that never moved down

Normally, after a tooth comes in, the gum slowly moves down to uncover the crown and settles near the CEJ (passive eruption). In altered passive eruption it doesn't, so teeth look short. It's graded two ways. Type 1: a wide band of gum, with the MGJ below the bone edge. Type 2: a normal band, with the MGJ at the CEJ. A: the bone is more than 1 mm below the CEJ. B: the bone is right up near the CEJ. Types 1A and 1B are the most common.

The fix is crown lengthening: 1A, cut away gum (gingivectomy); 2A, move the gum down with a flap (apically positioned flap); 1B and 2B, the flap plus bone reshaping. Why: in a B type the bone is too close, so it has to be moved; in Type 2 the gum band is only normal width, so cutting it away would leave too little firm gum, and the flap moves it down instead. Only 1A has extra gum and room above the bone.

Before crown lengthening

The clinical crown is what shows above the gum; the anatomical crown is all the enamel, down to the CEJ. Check the pocket depths, gum health and width of firm gum, and on the radiograph how deep any fracture or decay goes, the root's length and shape, where the bone is, and whether the nerve is involved.

Checking the smile

His checklist: face symmetry (the face in thirds; the face's midline against the teeth's midline; a long lower third means the upper jaw grew too far down); smile line (high, medium or low); edges of the front teeth (they should follow the lower lip); upper lip (20-22 mm in women, 22-24 mm in men, and it normally lifts 6-8 mm in a full smile); gum line (the central incisors and canines level, the lateral incisors 1 mm lower, toward the biting edge); and tooth shape and proportions: the golden proportion, so from the front the central, lateral and the visible part of the canine show at about 1.618 : 1 : 0.618 (the guide rounds it to 1.6, 1 and 0.6).

Treating a gummy smile

By cause: short teeth (altered passive eruption): crown lengthening and restorations; upper jaw too long: braces and jaw surgery, maybe with gum surgery too; lip that lifts too far: lip repositioning surgery or Botox; short upper lip: no good options. If there are several causes, combine treatments.

Patient 1

A healthy 28-year-old woman who didn't like the color of her front teeth (fluorosis), didn't want braces and wanted veneers. Her face thirds were equal and her lip was normal in length and movement, but she had a high smile line, an uneven, tilted gum line and short, square front teeth. So her gummy smile came from the teeth and gums, not the jaw or lip, and the plan was crown lengthening, then veneers. The photos follow her healing out to 18 months.

Discolored gum

The last problem on the list: a gray stain in the gum, a tattoo. The slides show one case where the stained tissue was cut out, replaced with a graft from the palate and reshaped 3 months later.

hy.diagnosis-tx-planning:
1 Stage from CAL and bone loss, never from probing depth alone

A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Never assign a stage from probing depth alone — confirm attachment loss and bone loss first. This was repeated twice in lecture, which is normally a signal of exam importance.

Every periodontal diagnosis starts with the same three numbers. Probing depth (PD) is measured from the gingival margin to the base of the pocket. Gingival recession (GR) is measured from the CEJ to the gingival margin. Clinical attachment level (CAL) — the number that actually matters for staging — is the sum of the two, effectively the distance from the CEJ to the base of the pocket. When the CEJ sits below the margin (no visible recession), GR is recorded as a negative number and CAL comes out smaller than PD; when recession is visible, GR is positive and CAL comes out larger than PD. A 7 mm pocket with the CEJ felt 4 mm subgingival is only 3 mm of attachment loss, while a shallow 2 mm pocket sitting on 4 mm of visible recession is 6 mm of attachment loss — more attachment loss on paper, but a far more maintainable tooth, because the patient can actually reach it with a brush.

Staging captures how severe the disease is and how complex it will be to manage, using interdental CAL as the gold standard (radiographic bone loss as a second choice). Stage 1 and 2 track rising CAL and bone loss in the coronal third of the root; Stage 3 and 4 both involve CAL ≥5 mm and bone loss into the middle third or beyond — the two are separated not by more attachment loss, but by tooth loss count (≤4 teeth lost pushes Stage 3, ≥5 pushes Stage 4) and by whether the case needs complex, multidisciplinary rehabilitation. Three findings force a case straight to Stage 3/4 regardless of the CAL math: vertical bone loss ≥3 mm, Class II–III furcation involvement, and any tooth loss attributable to periodontitis. A recurring pitfall: a deep probing depth by itself never proves periodontitis — without confirmed bone loss, a mouthful of 4s and 5s could just be generalized gingivitis.

2 Grading: start at B; the bone-loss/age ratio, smoking and HbA1c

Midterm check-ins · 7 questions in the bank

Grading estimates how fast the disease is moving and how the patient is likely to respond. The default assumption is Grade B (moderate), shifted up or down only with evidence. Where serial records exist, direct evidence of progression over time is the gold standard; otherwise, percent bone loss on the worst tooth divided by the patient's age gives a ratio — under 0.25 suggests Grade A, 0.25–1.0 suggests Grade B, and over 1.0 suggests Grade C. Two modifiers can only push the grade up: heavy smoking (more than 10 cigarettes a day) and an HbA1c of 7% or higher both bump a case to Grade C outright, even if the bone-loss/age ratio alone would suggest B. A patient never earns a downgrade simply for not smoking or not having diabetes. Only one stage and one grade are assigned per patient — the stage comes from the single worst site in the mouth, and the grade from progression evidence plus modifiers.

3 Stage 4 complexity factors (the 2018 AAP/EFP tables)

Midterm check-ins · 5 questions in the bank

Explained under 1 above: Stage from CAL and bone loss, never from probing depth alone

4 Caries control is part of Phase I; the treatment sequence

A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Caries control is bundled into Phase I therapy, not deferred until after SRP or surgery.

Every patient starts with Phase I (non-surgical) therapy, regardless of stage: oral hygiene instruction, scaling and root planing, smoking-cessation counseling, replacement of plaque-retentive restorative margins, and — easy to forget — caries control, restored before or alongside SRP rather than deferred, since a cavitated surface is harder to clean and instrument. Any permanent crown or final RPD waits until periodontal therapy is complete; a temporary crown bridges the gap. The Phase I re-evaluation appointment, not the initial exam, is where the definitive call on surgical (Phase II) therapy gets made, based on how much the tissue improved and how well the patient complied. Stage 1–2 cases often resolve with Phase I alone and move straight to maintenance; Stage 3–4 cases more often need Phase II — resective surgery to recontour bone into a physiologic, cleansable shape, or regenerative surgery to rebuild a favorable defect. Every plan ends in maintenance, and the evidence for it is stark: patients who refuse treatment lose roughly three times as many teeth as treated patients, and even treated patients who skip maintenance lose teeth at about twice the rate of those who keep their recall visits.

5 Maintenance works: the Becker tooth-loss figures

A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank

The periodontium itself can be intact or reduced, independent of disease activity. An intact periodontium can be healthy or have gingivitis. A reduced periodontium — from prior periodontitis, crown lengthening, or simple recession — can also be healthy or inflamed. A previously treated periodontitis patient who is stable on maintenance is diagnosed as healthy on a reduced periodontium, not re-staged, unless disease recurs; if pockets deepen and bleeding returns at a later maintenance visit, the diagnosis shifts back toward periodontitis depending on how widespread the change is.

6 Patient Box cases: stage and grade from the box

Midterm check-ins · 10 questions in the bank

Health means no probing depth beyond 3 mm, no bleeding, and no attachment or bone loss. Plaque-induced gingivitis can still show probing depths of 4–5 mm and bleeding on probing, but critically no attachment loss and no bone loss — it is contained entirely within the gingiva and is fully reversible with plaque control. A 10% bleeding-on-probing threshold across the full mouth is used before calling a case gingivitis, since probing pressure varies enough between examiners that two or three isolated bleeding sites should not trigger the diagnosis on their own. Periodontitis is different: attachment loss and bone loss are both present, pockets often reach 6 mm or more, and — unlike gingivitis — the disease is not fully reversible. Treatment can stabilize a periodontitis patient, but the best achievable outcome is health on a reduced periodontium, not a full return to the original attachment level.

7 Recession types from the chart: RT1, RT2, RT3 and root coverage

Midterm check-ins · 5 questions in the bank

Recession can occur in tissue that has never had periodontitis, so it is classified separately by how much interproximal attachment is also lost. RT1 has no interproximal loss at all and predicts full root coverage. RT2 has some interproximal loss, but buccal recession still exceeds it, predicting partial coverage. RT3 has interproximal loss that exceeds the buccal recession, and root coverage is not attempted because it will not succeed.

On multiple-answer items, pick only what you're sure of, since wrong picks can cost credit.
